children.translated_text: Introduction.

children.text:
asminbharatakhaṇḍe khalvadyāvadhi bahavaḥ saṃskṛtagranthāḥ saṃśodhya mudraṇadvārā prākāśyaṃ nītāstatra tatra paṇḍitaprakāṇḍaiḥ /
tathāpi katicana prājīnāḥ prabandhāḥ prakāśanārhā api pustakakośeṣveva nilīnā vartante /
teṣāmanyatamo 'yaṃ kāvyālaṅkārasaṃgrahākhyaḥ prabandho yo 'dya mahatā prayatnena sahṛdayahṛdayavanodāya prakāśyate /
children.translated_text: In this land of <s>Bhārata</s>, indeed, up to the present day, many Sanskrit works have been edited and brought to light through printing by eminent scholars here and there. Even so, several ancient compositions, though worthy of publication, remain hidden in manuscript libraries. One such composition is this work entitled <s>Kāvyālaṅkārasaṃgraha</s> (Compendium of Poetic Ornaments), which is now being published with great effort for the delight of the hearts of connoisseurs (<s>sahṛdaya</s>).

children.text:
asya kāvyālaṅkārasaṅgrahagranthasya praṇetā udbhaṭabhaṭṭaḥ /
udbhaṭabhaṭṭasya bhaṭṭodbhaṭaudbhaṭācāryaḥ
children.translated_text: The author of this work, the <s>Kāvyālaṅkārasaṅgraha</s>, is <s>Udbhaṭa Bhaṭṭa</s>. <s>Udbhaṭa Bhaṭṭa</s> [is also known as] <s>Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa</s> [and] <s>Udbhaṭācārya</s> —

children.text:
ityāpi nāmollekho granthāntareṣu dṛśyate /
udbhaṭabhaṭṭa kaśmīreṣu jayāpīḍaḥ bhūpasya sabhāpatirāsīditi kalhaṇavaracatarājataraṅgiṇīgranthādavagamyate /
jayāpīḍanṛpatirājyakālastu khrista 779 varṣamārabhya 813 varṣaparyantamāsīditi jñāyate /
atastatsabhāpaterudbhaṭabhaṭṭasyāpi jīvitasamayaḥ sa eveti viduṣāṃ nirṇayaḥ /
children.translated_text: such name-references are also seen in other works. It is understood from the <s>Rājataraṅgiṇī</s> composed by <s>Kalhaṇa</s> that <s>Udbhaṭa Bhaṭṭa</s> was the president of the court of King <s>Jayāpīḍa</s> in <s>Kaśmīra</s>. The reign of King <s>Jayāpīḍa</s> is known to have extended from the year 779 CE to 813 CE. Therefore, the lifetime of the court president <s>Udbhaṭa Bhaṭṭa</s> was the same — this is the conclusion of the learned.

children.text:
udbhaṭācāryeṇa kumārasaṃbhavākhyaṃ kāvyaṃ tathā bhāmahakṛtālaṅkāragranthasya vivaraṇaṃ ca viracitamāsīditi jñāyate /
atra pramāṇaṃ tu asyāṃ laghuvṛttau "anena granthakṛtā khoparacitakumārasaṃbhavaikadeśo 'tra udāharaṇatvenopanyastaḥ"pṛ0 15 iti "viśeṣoktalakṣaṇe ca bhāmahavivaraṇe bhaṭṭodbhaṭena ekadeśaśbada evaṃ vyākhyātaḥ"pṛ0 13 iti ca pratīhārendurājasyoktiḥ /
children.translated_text: <s>Udbhaṭācārya</s> is known to have composed a poem called <s>Kumārasaṃbhava</s> and also a commentary (<s>vivaraṇa</s>) on the ornament-treatise composed by <s>Bhāmaha</s>. The evidence for this is the statement of <s>Pratīhārendurāja</s> in this short commentary (<s>laghuvṛtti</s>): 'A portion of the <s>Kumārasaṃbhava</s> composed by this author of the treatise has been cited here as an illustration' (p. 15), and 'In the <s>Bhāmahavivaraṇa</s>, regarding the definition stated with a specific qualifier, <s>Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa</s> has explained the word "ekadeśa" (a portion) in this manner' (p. 13).

children.text: kāvyālaṅkārasāralaghuvṛtteḥ praṇetā śrīpratahārendurājastu koṅkaṇadeśavāstavyaḥ kaśmīreṣu mīmāṃsākhyākaraṇatarkasāhityaśāstrapāraṃgatabhaṭṭaśrīmukulādadhītaśāstraśceti asyā laghuvṛtteḥ prārambhopasaṃhārayoḥ sthitābhyāṃ nimnalikhitapadyābhyāṃ sphuṭaṃ bhavati /
children.translated_text: The author of the <s>Kāvyālaṅkārasāralaghuvṛtti</s> (Short Commentary on the Essence of Poetic Ornaments), <s>Śrī Pratīhārendurāja</s>, was a resident of the <s>Koṅkaṇa</s> region and had studied the sciences (<s>śāstra</s>) under <s>Bhaṭṭa Śrī Mukula</s>, who was proficient in <s>Mīmāṃsā</s>, grammar (<s>vyākaraṇa</s>), logic (<s>tarka</s>), and literary science (<s>sāhitya</s>) in <s>Kaśmīra</s> — this becomes clear from the following two verses placed at the beginning and conclusion of this short commentary:
"Having studied under <s>Mukula</s>, foremost among the learned, it is analyzed
by <s>Pratīhārendurāja</s> — the <s>Kāvyālaṅkārasaṃgraha</s>."
"From <s>Mīmāṃsā</s>, the cloud of essence; from the ocean of <s>Pada</s> [grammar]; from the jewel-casket of logic (<s>tarka</s>);
from <s>Murāri</s>, the glory of literary science; from the bee at the feet of <s>Śauri</s>, the intoxicating flower of the learned;
having heard from <s>Mukula</s>, the ocean of generosity, the best banner, the irrigating channel of the creeper of fame,
the <s>Koṅkaṇa</s> native <s>Śrī Indurāja</s> composed this short commentary on the <s>Kāvyālaṅkārasāra</s>."
Thus.

children.text:
pratīhārendurājasya jīvitakālastu niścitya vaktuṃ na śakyate /
tathāpyayaṃ bhaṭṭodbhasya paścādbabhūveti vyaktameva /
anena laghuvṛttau bhāmaha--vāmana---udbhaṭa---ityādi prācīnālaṅkārikāṇāmevollekhaḥ kṛtaḥ natu mahimabhaṭṭa-ānandavardhana-kāvyaprakāśakārādyabhinavālaṅkārikāṇām /
ato 'yaṃ khistavarṣasya navamadaśamaśatakayormadhye babhūveti tarkyate /
children.translated_text: The exact lifetime of <s>Pratīhārendurāja</s> cannot be determined with certainty. Nevertheless, it is clear that he came after <s>Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa</s>. In his short commentary, he mentions only earlier rhetoricians (<s>alaṅkārikas</s>) such as <s>Bhāmaha</s>, <s>Vāmana</s>, <s>Udbhaṭa</s>, etc., but not later rhetoricians such as <s>Mahimabhaṭṭa</s>, <s>Ānandavardhana</s>, the author of the <s>Kāvyaprakāśa</s>, and others. Therefore, it is conjectured that he lived between the ninth and tenth centuries CE.

children.text: asya granthasyādarśapustakamekameva puṇyapattanasthārājakīyapustakālayādhikāribhiḥ prophesara vināyaka sakhārāma ghāṭe ityetai saṃskaraṇārthe datvanṛgṛhīto 'smīti kṛtajñatayā smarāmi teṣāmupakṛtim /
children.translated_text: The single manuscript copy of this work was given by the authorities of the Royal Library at <s>Puṇyapattana</s> (Pune) to Professor <s>Vināyaka Sakhārāma Ghāṭe</s> for editing, and I gratefully recall their assistance in this matter.
In the city of <s>Kāravāra</s> (Karwar), a humble attendant of the learned,
<s>Śrāvaṇa śu.</s> 12, <s>Śake</s> 1837 — <s>Maṅgeśa Śarmā</s>.
Auspiciousness! The <s>Kāvyālaṅkārasaṃgraha</s> (Compendium of Poetic Ornaments) composed by the illustrious <s>Udbhaṭa Bhaṭṭa</s>.
First Section, accompanied by the <s>Kāvyālaṅkārasāralaghuvṛtti</s> (Short Commentary on the Essence of Poetic Ornaments) composed by the illustrious <s>Pratīhārendurāja</s>.
That which is made white by the white laughter of <s>Lakṣmī</s>, who indulges in the sport of witty speech (<s>narmoktilīlā</s>), belonging to <s>Śauri</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>),
and which is somewhere pinkish due to the abundant radiance of the <s>Kaustubha</s> gem with its spreading rays,
and which elsewhere is dappled by the golden-hued splendor of the garment of heaven,
that chest [of <s>Viṣṇu</s>], resembling the sky adorned with an unbroken rainbow, may it protect the world! (1)
When the demon-enemy (<s>Mahiṣāsura</s>) was slain, [you showed] fearlessness to the celestial dwellings, having displayed terror [to the demon];
O <s>Gaurī</s>, I bow to your pair of feet, which delight <s>Indra</s> and are honored. (2)
Having studied under <s>Mukula</s>, foremost among the learned, it is analyzed
by <s>Pratīhārendurāja</s> — the <s>Kāvyālaṅkārasaṃgraha</s>. (3)
<s>Punaruktavadābhāsa</s> (semblance of repetition), and <s>chekānuprāsa</s> (elegant alliteration),
<s>Anuprāsa</s> (alliteration) is threefold, <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s> (Lāṭa alliteration), and <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) is fourfold. (1.1)
<s>Upamā</s> (simile), and <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination), and likewise <s>prativastūpamā</s> (counter-object simile),
these alone are the ornaments of speech enumerated by some. (1.2)

children.text:
atrālaṅkārā aṣṭāvuddiṣṭāḥ /
tatrādau catvāraḥ śabdālaṅkārā nirūpitāḥ /
rūpakādīnāṃ tu caturṇāmatra arthālaṅkāratā /
atrānuprāse rūpake yathākramaṃ tridheti caturiti vacanaṃ vipratipattinirāsārtham /
bhāmaho hi grāmyopanāgarakāvṛttabhedena dviprakāramevānuprāsaṃ vyākhyātavān /
tathā rūpakasya ye catvāro bhedā vakṣyante tanmadhyādādyameva bhedadvitayaṃ prādarśayat /
ataḥ svābhimatabhedopadarśanadvāreṇa evaṃvidhavipratipattinirāsārthamuddeśāvasthāyāmevānuprāsastridheti rūpakaṃ caturiti coktam /
rūpakaṃ caturityatra
children.translated_text: Here eight ornaments have been enumerated. Among these, the first four are <s>śabdālaṅkāras</s> (ornaments of sound) that have been defined. But the four beginning with <s>rūpaka</s> etc. are <s>arthālaṅkāras</s> (ornaments of meaning). Here, the statements 'threefold' regarding <s>anuprāsa</s> and 'fourfold' regarding <s>rūpaka</s> are for the purpose of removing misapprehension. For <s>Bhāmaha</s> explained <s>anuprāsa</s> as being of only two kinds, distinguished by the categories of rustic (<s>grāmya</s>), refined (<s>upanāgaraka</s>), and elegant (<s>vṛtta</s>). Similarly, of the four varieties of <s>rūpaka</s> that will be stated, he had shown only the first two. Therefore, in order to remove such misapprehensions by showing his own preferred varieties, it was stated at the enumeration stage itself that '<s>anuprāsa</s> is threefold' and '<s>rūpaka</s> is fourfold.' Regarding 'rūpaka is fourfold' —

children.text:
rūpakatvena saha ekasminnarthe vartamānā sattā rūpakedeṣvāvartamānā pratīyate /
ataḥ pratīyamānā yāsau rūpakatvaikārthasamavetā sattātmikā bhavanakriyā tadabhyāvṛttāvayaṃ "dvitricaturbhyaḥ suc"(pā. a. 5.4.18) iti sucpratyayaḥ /
rūpakaṃ caturṣu bhedeṣu caturo vārān bhedātmanā bhavatītyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The existence (<s>sattā</s>) that occurs together with the nature of <s>rūpaka</s> in one meaning is understood as recurring in the varieties of <s>rūpaka</s>. Therefore, the <s>suc</s> suffix [is applied] according to the rule '<s>dvitricaturbhyaḥ suc</s>' (<s>Pāṇini</s> 5.4.18) for the repeated occurrence of the existential verbal action that is co-present with the single meaning of <s>rūpaka</s>-ness. The meaning is: <s>rūpaka</s> occurs in four varieties, being fourfold in the form of [its] varieties.
Among these, <s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s> (semblance of repetition) is now explained —
<s>Punaruktābhāsa</s> (semblance of repetition) appears as if referring to the same object, [yet its] words are of different form.

children.text:
abhinnaṃ vastu yasminnudbhāsate tadabhinnavastu /
bhinnaṃ rūpaṃ yayoḥ padayoste bhinnarūpe /
abhinnavastviva abhīkṣṇamudbhāsete bhinnarūpe pade yasmiṃstadabhinnavastvivodbhāsibhinnarūpapadam /
evamayaṃ bahuvrīhidvitayagarbhaḥ pañcapadobahuvrīhiḥ /
tatraiko 'bhinnavastviti bahuvrīhiḥ /
aparastu bhinnarūpa iti /
tadgarbhaścāyaṃ bahuvrīhirabhinnavastvivodbhāsibhinnarūpapadamiti /
anena ca yatra bhinnarūpe pade ekārthavadābhāsete tatpunaruktābhāsaṃ kāvyamalaṅkāryaṃ nirdiṣṭam /
yadyapi /
punaruktavadābhāsamityuddeśe vatiḥ prayuktastathāpi tasyeha gamyamānārthatvādaprayogaḥ /
uddeśe tvevamanabhidhānamabhidhāvaicitryapradarśanārtham /
kācit khalu gamyamānārthanvayena abhidhā
children.translated_text: 'Identical object' (<s>abhinnavast</s>) means that in which an identical object shines forth. 'Different form' (<s>bhinnarūpa</s>) means two words whose forms are different. [The compound means:] that in which words of different form repeatedly shine forth as if [referring to] an identical object — this is '<s>abhinnavastvivodbhāsibhinnarūpapadam</s>.' Thus, this is a five-member <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound containing two <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compounds. One is the <s>bahuvrīhi</s> '<s>abhinnavastu</s>' (identical object). The other is '<s>bhinnarūpa</s>' (different form). And the <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound containing these is '<s>abhinnavastvivodbhāsibhinnarūpapadam</s>.' By this, wherever two words of different form appear as if synonymous, that poetry to be adorned has been defined as <s>punaruktābhāsa</s>. Even though the suffix <s>vat</s> was used in the enumeration as '<s>punaruktavadābhāsam</s>,' since its meaning is already understood here, it is not employed [again]. In the enumeration, however, such non-expression is for the purpose of showing the variety of expression. Indeed, some expression

children.text:
pravartate, kācittvabhidhīyamānārthanvayena /
tatroddeśe vatyabhidhīyamānasādṛśyānvayena abhidhā upadarśitā /
iha tvarthasāmarthyavaseyasādṛśyānvayena /
tadevamarthasāmarthyāvaseyena vatyarthenānvitaṃ punaruktābhāsamatra kāvyamalaṅkāryaṃ yatkāvyaṃ taddharmatvena punaruktavadābhāsamānayoḥ padayoralaṅkāratvamuktaṃ na tu svatantratayā /
phalaṃ caivamabhidhānasya punaruktavadābhāsamānapadasamanvayasya alaṅkāratākhyāpanam /
alaṅkārasya khalvalaṅkāryaparatantratayā nirūpaṇe kriyamāṇe suṣṭhu svarūpaṃ nirūpitaṃ bhavati /
svātmanyavasthitasya tasyānalaṅkāratvāt /
samudgakasthitahārakeyūrapārihāryādyalaṅkāravat /
ataḥ punaruktavadābhāsatvusyālaṅkaratākhyāpanāya kāvyaparatantratayā nirdeśo yukta eva /
children.translated_text: operates through connection with the understood meaning, while another operates through connection with the expressed meaning. Therein, in the enumeration, the expression was shown through connection with expressed similarity [using <s>vat</s>]. But here, [the similarity is grasped] through connection with similarity to be inferred from the force of meaning. Thus, <s>punaruktābhāsa</s> here is the poetry to be adorned, connected with the meaning of <s>vat</s> inferable from the force of meaning — the ornament-status of these two words, <s>punaruktavadābhāsamāna</s>, is stated as a property of the poetry, not independently. And the result of such expression — of the connection of the word <s>punaruktavadābhāsamāna</s> — is the indication of ornament-status. For when an ornament is defined in dependence on the object to be adorned, its own nature is well defined, since it is not an ornament when existing by itself — like a necklace, armlet, or bangle ornament kept in a box. Therefore, the definition [of <s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s>] in dependence on the poetry [it adorns] is entirely appropriate for indicating its ornament-status.
An illustration of this —
From that time on, the wearer of the elephant-hide, free from attachment,
the blue-throated one (<s>Śitikaṇṭha</s>, i.e. <s>Śiva</s>), was afflicted by the fire of grief over [the death of] <s>Satī</s>, whose life departed with time. (1.*1)

children.text:
tadāprabhṛti satīviyogādārabhya sa devaḥ śitikaṇṭho niḥsaṅgaḥ san divasānatavāhitavāniti vakṣyamāṇe śloke vākyārthaparisamāptiḥ /
kṛttiścarma /
kālavaśena nivartamānā (yā) satī (tasyāḥ) viyogena janito yaḥ śokavahnistadudbhavā pīḍā yasya sa tathoktaḥ /
atra nāgakuñjaraśabdau śitikaṇṭhakālagalaśabdau ca punaruktavadābhāsete /
tathāhi /
nāgakuñcaraśabdayorupaktamāvasthāyāṃ gajavācitvena ekārthatvaṃ pratibhāti /
padārthanvayaparyālocanayā tu tadbādhyate /
nāgaśabdaḥ khalvatra hastivācī /
kuñcaraśabdastu tatpraśaṃsāvagatahetuḥ /
evaṃ śitikaṇṭhakālagalaśabdayorapi
children.translated_text: 'From that time' means from the separation from <s>Satī</s> onwards, that god, the blue-throated one, being free from attachment, spent his days — the completion of the sentence-meaning occurs in the verse to follow. <s>Kṛtti</s> means skin. 'Departed with time' — <s>Satī</s> who passed away by the force of time; the grief-fire born from her separation; the affliction arising from that — he is described thus. Here, the words <s>nāga</s> and <s>kuñjara</s>, and the words <s>śitikaṇṭha</s> and <s>kālagala</s>, appear as semblances of repetition. For: when the words <s>nāga</s> and <s>kuñjara</s> are first encountered, synonymity in denoting 'elephant' is apprehended. But upon analyzing the connection of word-meanings, that [synonymity] is overridden. The word <s>nāga</s> here means 'elephant,' while the word <s>kuñjara</s> becomes the basis for understanding praise of it. Similarly, regarding the words <s>śitikaṇṭha</s> and <s>kālagala</s> —

children.text:
valīviśeṣāvacchinnaśarīrāvayavabhedopetārthābhidhāyitvātpaunaruktyaṃ saṃbhāvyamānaṃ kālagaladiti takārāvadhiparyālocanayā cāpasāryate /
tenātra punaruktābhāsatvam /
children.translated_text: since [both] denote meanings endowed with distinctions of body-parts delimited by specific markings, the suspicion of repetition is entertained, but it is then dispelled by analyzing [the compound] <s>kālagala</s> up to the letter 'ta' [i.e., <s>kāla</s> = time, <s>gala</s> = throat, not merely 'black-throated']. Hence there is semblance of repetition (<s>punaruktābhāsa</s>) here.

children.text:
nanu chekānuprāsalakṣaṇādanantaraṃ punaruktavadābhāsodāharaṇaṃ paṭhyate /
tatkathaṃ punaruktavadābhāsalakṣaṇavyākhyānasamaya eva tasyopanyāsaḥ kṛtaḥ /
ucyate /
udāharaṇapradarśanamantareṇa lakṣaṇārthasya duradhigamatvādihaiva tadupanyastamityadoṣaḥ /
evamuttaratrāpi prameyaśabdānusāreṇa granthapāṭhakramaviparyāsena vyākhyāyāṃ nāsūyitavyam /
pāṭhakramādārthakramasya balīyastvāt /
children.translated_text: Now, the illustration of <s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s> is read after the definition of <s>chekānuprāsa</s>. So how can it be presented at the very time of explaining the definition of <s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s>? It is answered: Because the meaning of the definition is difficult to grasp without showing the illustration, it has been presented here itself — there is no fault. Similarly, even hereafter, when the commentary proceeds in an order different from the text's reading order, following the sequence of subject matter, one should not find fault — for the sequence of meaning is stronger than the sequence of reading.
<s>Chekānuprāsa</s> (elegant alliteration) —
<s>Chekānuprāsa</s> is when well-matched utterance is achieved in pairs. (1.3)

children.text:
dvayordvayorajjhalsamudāyayoḥ suṣṭhu sadṛśe uccāraṇe kriyamāṇe sati chekānuprāso bhavati /
tathāvidhā samudāyāstatrālaṅkāratāṃ pratipadyante /
dvayordvayoriti svārthe 'vadhāryamāṇe anekasminniti dvirvacanaṃ svārthagrahaṇena vīpsāyā nirastatvāt na yāvanto 'tra dvikāḥ saṃbhavanti teṣāṃ sarveṣāmeva susadṛśatvaṃ kāryaṃ, kiṃ tarhi katipayānāmeva /
vīpsā hi sākalye sati bhavati /
sā cātra svārthaśabdena nirastā /
avadhāryamāṇagrahaṇācca dvayordvayorevātra samudāyayoḥ sadṛśatvaṃ, natu trayāṇāṃ trayāṇāmiti draṣṭavyam /
anekasminniti vacanācca asakṛdevaṃvidharūpopanibandhe sati chekānuprāsatā na tu sakṛditi mantavyam /
parasparamekarūpānvitā
children.translated_text: When well-matched pronunciation is produced in pairs of pairs of vowel-consonant groups, <s>chekānuprāsa</s> occurs. Such groups therein attain ornament-status. 'In pairs of pairs' — when this is understood in its own sense, [it means] 'in many [pairs]'; the reduplication [of <s>dvayoḥ</s>] is not for the purpose of totality (since totality is set aside by the word's own sense), so it is not necessary that all possible pairs be well-matched — rather, only some [need be]. For totality-conveying repetition (<s>vīpsā</s>) occurs when completeness is intended, but here that is set aside by the word's own sense. And because of the limiting sense [of <s>dvayoḥ</s>], the similarity is between pairs of groups specifically, not among threes and threes. And because of the word 'in many [instances],' <s>chekānuprāsa</s> obtains when such a pattern of similar forms is present more than once, not just once. Mutually endowed with uniform character,

children.text:
rasādyabhivyaktyanuguṇatvena labdhotkarṣā varṇāstatsamudāyā vā śobhātiśayahetutvena kāvye kṣiṣyamāṇā anuprāsaśabdenānvarthenābhidhīyante /
chekaśabdena kulāyābhiratānāṃ pakṣiṇāmabhidhānam /
taduktam---"chekān gṛheṣvabhiratānuśanti mṛgapakṣiṇaḥ"iti /
teṣāṃ ca kulāyābhiratatvādanyena kenacidanāyāsyamānānāmanenānuprāsena sadṛśī madhurā vāguccarati /
ato 'yamanuprāsaśchekairvyapadiśyate chekānuprāsa iti /
athavā chekā vidagdhāḥ /
tadvallabhatvādasya chekānuprāsatā /
tasyodāharaṇam----
children.translated_text: letters whose excellence is attained through suitability for the expression of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion) and the like, or groups of them, when placed in poetry as causes of heightened beauty — these are denoted by the word <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration) in its etymological sense. The word <s>cheka</s> denotes birds that delight in their nests. As stated: 'The <s>chekas</s> are said to be animals and birds that delight in their homes.' Since they delight in their nests and are not enticed by anything else, speech similar to them is sweet with this alliteration. Therefore this alliteration is designated by the <s>chekas</s>, hence '<s>chekānuprāsa</s>.' Alternatively, <s>cheka</s> means 'the refined/connoisseurs.' Because it is dear to them, it is <s>chekānuprāsa</s>. An illustration of this —
That god spent his days in that cave of the lord of mountains,
attended by foremost <s>Pramathas</s> (Śiva's attendants) of the most weighty assemblies. (1.*2)

children.text:
kandaro guhā /
gariṣṭhā gurutamāḥ /
'priyasthira-'(pā.a.6.4.157) itīṣṭhani guruśabdasya garādeśaḥ /
goṣṭhī vidagdhānāmāsanabandhaḥ /
prathamaiḥ pradhānaiḥ /
pramathairgaṇaiḥ /
paryupāsitaḥ sevitaḥ /
atra sadevadivasaśabdau indrakandaraśabdau gariṣṭhagoṣṭhīśabdau prathamapramathaśabdau pariupāsaśabdau ca dvau dvau ajjhalsamudāyau susadṛśāvṛccāritau tena chekānuprāsatā /
kvacittu 'ninye tasmin'ityatra 'ninye 'nyasmin'iti pāṭhaḥ /
tadā caitadapyudāharaṇe 'ntarbhavatīti /
children.translated_text: <s>Kandara</s> means cave. <s>Gariṣṭha</s> means 'most weighty,' by the substitution of <s>gar</s> for <s>guru</s> before the superlative suffix <s>iṣṭhan</s> according to the rule '<s>priyasthira-</s>' (<s>Pāṇini</s> 6.4.157). <s>Goṣṭhī</s> means an assembly of the refined. <s>Prathama</s> means foremost. <s>Pramatha</s> means attendants [of <s>Śiva</s>]. <s>Paryupāsita</s> means served/attended upon. Here, the words <s>sa-deva</s> and <s>divasa</s>, <s>indra</s> and <s>kandara</s>, <s>gariṣṭha</s> and <s>goṣṭhī</s>, <s>prathama</s> and <s>pramatha</s>, and <s>pari</s> and <s>upāsa</s> — each pair of vowel-consonant groups is pronounced in well-matched fashion, hence <s>chekānuprāsa</s>. In some [manuscripts], however, in the phrase '<s>ninye tasmin</s>,' the reading is '<s>ninye 'nyasmin</s>.' In that case, this too would be included within the illustration.

children.text:
anuprāsaḥ /
sa ca trividho vṛttisaṃśrayāt /
yadvakṣyati-----
children.translated_text: <s>Anuprāsa</s> (alliteration): It is threefold because it depends on [three] <s>vṛttis</s> (styles). As will be stated —
"The placement of similar consonants in each of these three <s>vṛttis</s> (styles) — poets always call that <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration), each separately."

children.text:
asyārthaḥ----
triṣveteṣu yathāyogaṃ rasādyabhivyaktyanuguṇeṣu varṇavyavahāreṣuyaḥ sarūpāṇāṃ vyañjanānāṃ pṛthak pṛthagupanibandhastamanuprāsaṃ kavayaḥ sadecchantīti /
atastāstāvadvṛttyo rasādyabhivyaktyanuguṇavarṇavyavahārātmikāḥ prathamamabhidhīyante /
tāśca tisraḥ, paruṣopanāgarikāgrāmyatvabhedāt /
children.translated_text: The meaning of this is: In each of these three modes of phonetic usage appropriate to the expression of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion) and the like, the separate placement of similar consonants — this the poets always desire as <s>anuprāsa</s>. Therefore, those <s>vṛttis</s>, consisting of phonetic usage appropriate to the expression of <s>rasa</s> and the like, are first defined. And they are three, distinguished by the categories: harsh (<s>paruṣa</s>), refined (<s>upanāgarika</s>), and rustic (<s>grāmya</s>).
Among these, the harsh (<s>paruṣa</s>) style —
Combined with [the consonants] <s>śa</s> and <s>ṣa</s>, conjuncts with <s>ra</s>, the <s>ṭa</s>-class,

children.text: paraṣā nāma vṛttiḥ syāt hlahvahyādyaiśca saṃyutā // UKss_1.4 //
children.translated_text: and joined with <s>hla</s>, <s>ha</s>, <s>hya</s>, and the like — this is the style called <s>paruṣā</s> (harsh). (1.4)

children.text:
śakāraṣakārādiyuktau varṇavyavahāraḥ paruṣākhyā vṛttiḥ /
rephopalakṣitāḥ saṃyogāḥ krarkādayo rephasaṃyogāḥ /
ṭakāropalakṣito vargaṣṭavargaḥ ṭaṭhaḍaḍhaṇeti /
asyāṃ vṛttau yo 'nuprāsaḥ sa paruṣānuprāsaḥ /
tasyodāharaṇam----
children.translated_text: When combined with the letters śa, ṣa, and the like, the usage of letters is called the <s>paruṣā</s> (harsh) style. Conjuncts marked by the letter ra, such as kra, rka, and so forth, are called repha-conjuncts. The ṭa-group, indicated by the letter ṭa, consists of ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa. The <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration) that occurs in this style is called <s>paruṣānuprāsa</s> (harsh alliteration). An example of that:
There, in the waters, with all the lotuses fully bloomed,
autumn shone, with the faces of the directions tawny from the awns of the rice stalks. [UKss 1.*3]

children.text:
toyāśayeṣu aśeṣaṃ sākalyena vyākośitāni vikāsitāni kuśeśayāni padmāni yayā iti samāsaḥ /
tathā śālīnāṃ dhānyānāṃ kiṃśārubhiḥ śūkaiḥ kapiśāni piñjarāṇi āśāmukhāni digavakāśā yasyāmiti samāsaḥ /
ayaṃ ca śakārasya sārūpyeṇopanibandhātparuṣānuprāsaḥ /
children.translated_text: The compound means: that [autumn] in which the <s>kuśeśayas</s> (lotuses) were completely, i.e., fully bloomed in the <s>toyāśayas</s> (bodies of water). Likewise, the compound means: that [autumn] in which the <s>āśāmukhas</s> (faces of the directions, i.e., the open spaces of the quarters) were <s>kapiśa</s> (tawny) from the <s>kiṃśārus</s> (awns) of the <s>śālīs</s> (rice plants). And this is <s>paruṣānuprāsa</s> because of the binding together of the letter śa in identical form.
<s>Apanāgarikā</s> (non-refined) [style]:
When combined with conjuncts of identical letters, and with stops (<s>sparśas</s>) joined by the last [nasals] of the groups at the top,

children.text: sparśairyutāṃ ca manyante upanāgarikāṃ budhāḥ // UKss_1.5 //
children.translated_text: the wise consider this the <s>upanāgarikā</s> (semi-refined) style. [UKss 1.5]

children.text:
sarūpāṇāṃ varṇānāṃ ye saṃyogāḥ kkappacca ityādayastairyuktā /
tathā vargāntyair ṅañaṇanamaiḥ ṅkañcaṇṭantampa-ityādirūpatayā upari ye yuktāḥ kādayo makārāntāḥ sparśāstairyuktā upanāgarikā vṛttiḥ /
eṣā khalu nāgarikayā vaidagdhījuṣā vanitayā upamīyate tata upanāgarikā /
nāgarikayā upamitā upanāgariketi /
"avādayaḥ ṛṣṭādyarthe tṛtīyayā"iti samāsaḥ /
tasyāmupanāgarikānuprāsaḥ /
tasyodāharaṇaṃ ca---
children.translated_text: Combined with conjuncts of identical letters, such as kka, ppa, cca, and so forth. Likewise, the stops from ka to ma — when combined above in the form ṅka, ñca, ṇṭa, nta, mpa, etc. with the final nasals of the groups (ṅa, ña, ṇa, na, ma) — constitute the <s>upanāgarikā</s> (semi-refined) style. Indeed, this [style] is compared to a <s>nāgarikā</s> (refined, city-dweller), a woman endowed with sophistication — hence it is called <s>upanāgarikā</s> (resembling the refined). 'Compared to the <s>nāgarikā</s> (refined)' — hence <s>upanāgarikā</s>. The compound follows the rule 'the <s>avādaya</s> [prefix upa-] in the sense of resemblance takes the third [case].' In that [style], the <s>upanāgarikānuprāsa</s> (semi-refined alliteration) [occurs]. An example of that:
With drops of nectar-water arising from dense clusters of lotuses,
flowing, with beautiful trembling, the bees were delighted somewhere. [UKss 1.*4]

children.text:
atra dakārākhyaḥ sparśo nakāreṇopari vyavasthitena yuktaḥ sārūpyeṇopanibaddhaḥ /
sāndrā ghanā aravindavṛndotthā makarandāmbubindava iti saṃbandhaḥ /
sundaraspandaṃ spandibhiriti sāmānyabhūtaḥ spandaḥ sundaraspandamiti viśiṣṭena spandena viśeṣito raipoṣaṃ puṣṇātītivat /
sundaraḥ spandoyasminniti hi sāmānyabhūte
children.translated_text: Here the stop called da, combined with the letter na positioned above it, is bound together in identical form. The connection is: the nectar-water-drops arising from dense clusters of lotuses were thick. '<s>Sundaraspanda</s>' (beautiful trembling) — <s>spanda</s> (trembling), being the general [quality], is specified by the particular trembling characterized as beautiful — like the expression 'nourishes beauty' (<s>raipoṣam</s>). 'Beautiful trembling in which' — thus, in the general sense of trembling belonging to another word,
the trembling qualified by beauty is the meaning of the compound word.
<s>Indindirā</s> means bees.
<s>Grāmya</s> (rustic) [style]:
With the remaining letters, appropriately, called by the name <s>komalā</s> (soft),
those of discerning intellect praise the <s>grāmya</s> (rustic) style in poetry. [UKss 1.6]

children.text:
paruṣopanāgarikopayuktavarṇāvaśiṣṭairvarṇairlakārādibhirupanibadhyamānā grāmyā /
tasyā eva ca aparaṃ nāmadheyaṃ komaleti /
komalākhyayā kathitāmiti saṃbandhaḥ /
tasyāṃ cānuprāso grāmyānuprāsaḥ /
tasyodāharaṇam----
children.translated_text: That which is bound together with the remaining letters such as la and others — remaining after those used in the <s>paruṣā</s> and <s>upanāgarikā</s> [styles] — is called <s>grāmyā</s>. And its other name is <s>komalā</s> (soft). The connection is: 'called by the name <s>komalā</s>.' And the alliteration in that [style] is <s>grāmyānuprāsa</s> (rustic alliteration). An example of that:
With the sweet sounds of playful, swaying rows of bees, somewhere
she created the illusion of the jingling of anklets belonging to the beauty ascending the forest. [UKss 1.*5]

children.text:
kelilolāḥ krīḍālampaṭāḥ /
kalairmadhuraiḥ /
bhramo bhrāntirviparyayapratyayaḥ /
atra lakārakakārarephāḥ sārūpyeṇopanibaddhāḥ /
evametāstisro vṛttayo vyākhyātāḥ /
tāsu ca rasādyabhivyaktyānuguṇyena pṛthak pṛthaganuprāso nibadhyate tadāha----
children.translated_text: <s>Kelilolāḥ</s> means those fond of amorous play. <s>Kalaiḥ</s> means with sweet [sounds]. <s>Bhrama</s> means delusion, a cognition of reversal. Here the letters la, ka, and ra are bound together in identical form. Thus these three styles have been explained. And in them, alliteration is employed separately in each, in conformity with the manifestation of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment) and the like. He says:
The placing of identical consonants in these three styles, each separately,
poets always call <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration). [UKss 1.7]
This verse has been explained with examples in the course of determining the nature of the styles.
<s>Lāṭānuprāsa</s> (Lāṭa alliteration):
Even when there is no difference in form and meaning, the repetition of words or phrases,

children.text: śabdānāṃ vā padānāṃ vā lāṭānuprāsa iṣyate // UKss_1.8 //
children.translated_text: because of a different purport, is considered <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s>. [UKss 1.8]
That [lāṭānuprāsa], by the occurrence of a pair of words, of two [words] or of one, as before,
because of the independence of the other, or because of one word being the basis for both — [UKss 1.9]
or because of the employment of both in the form of independent words,
it is divided in many ways by distinctions and by the sequence of <s>pāda</s> (verse-quarter) repetition. [UKss 1.10]

children.text: śabdānāmanupalabhyamānasuptiṅāṃ tathā padānāmupalabhyamānasuptiṅāṃ, ubhayeṣāṃ ca śabdapadānāṃ svarūpasya varṇātmanaḥ abhidheyasya ca nirantaraśabdavyāpāragocarīkṛtasya vācyasyārthasyābhede 'pi phalāntarāttātparyabhedāt punaruktiḥ sā lāṭadeśanivāsijanavallabhatvāllāṭānuprāso 'bhidhīyate /
children.translated_text: For words (<s>śabdas</s>) that do not have perceptible nominal or verbal endings, and for words (<s>padas</s>) that do have perceptible nominal or verbal endings, and for both words and padas — even when there is no difference in their form (i.e., their phonemic identity) and in their meaning (i.e., the referent that is the object of the continuous operation of words) — repetition due to a different purport, i.e., a difference in the intended import, is called <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s>, because it is favored by the people dwelling in the <s>Lāṭa</s> region.

children.text:
sa ca prathamaṃ tāvatrriprakāraḥ /
dvayoḥ svatantrayordvayoḥ paratantrayoḥ svatantraparatantrayośca bhāvāt /
tatra yasyāvaddvayoḥ svatantrayoḥ sa dviprakāraḥ /
ekaikasmin pade padasamudāyātmake ca pāde bhāvāt /
taduktam----
children.translated_text: And that [lāṭānuprāsa], first of all, is of three kinds — because there can be two independent [words], two dependent [words], or one independent and one dependent. Therein, that which involves two independent [words] is of two kinds — because it can occur in individual words or in a verse-quarter consisting of a collection of words. This was stated:
"Because of the employment of both in the form of independent words,
it is divided in many ways by distinctions and by the sequence of <s>pāda</s> (verse-quarter) repetition."
[Thus it is.]

children.text:
atra hi svatantrapadātmakatvena dvayoḥ prayogādekaikapadāśrayo lāṭānuprāso 'bhihitaḥ /
tasyodāharaṇam-----
children.translated_text: For here, through the employment of two [repetitions] in the form of independent words, the <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s> based on individual words is stated. An example of that:

children.text: kāśāḥ kāśā ivodbhānti sarāṃsīva sarāṃsi ca /
children.translated_text: The <s>kāśa</s> (grasses) shine forth like <s>kāśa</s> (grasses), and the lakes like lakes;
the rivers, like rivers, captivated the minds of the young. [UKss 1.*6]

children.text:
ācikṣipurapatdṛtavantaḥ /
atra kāśādayaḥ śabdā aparaiḥ kāśādibhiḥ śabdai ekarūpā ekābhidheyāśca /
tātparyabhedena tu teṣāṃ punaruktiḥ /
tathā hyatra ekeṣāṃ kāśādiśabdānāṃ jātibhedoparaktadravyaparatayā prayogaḥ /
apareṣāṃ tu ananvayālaṅkāracchāyayā upamānāntaravyāvṛttiparatayā /
atra ca svātantryaṃ padānāṃ, kāśādīnāmupalabhyamānasuptiṅrūpatvāt /
ekaikarūpatayā cāvṛtterupanibandhaḥ /
children.translated_text: <s>Ācikṣipuḥ</s> means they attracted. Here the words <s>kāśa</s> and the like are identical in form and identical in meaning with the other words <s>kāśa</s> and the like. But there is repetition due to a difference in purport. For here, of one set of <s>kāśa</s> and other words, the usage is with reference to the substance colored by the distinction of universal (<s>jāti</s>). Of the other set, however, [the usage is] with reference to the exclusion of other objects of comparison, with the suggestion of the figure of speech called <s>ananvaya</s> (self-comparison). And here the words are independent, because the forms <s>kāśa</s> and the like have perceptible nominal or verbal endings. The binding is accomplished through repetition of each individual [word].

children.text:
padasamudāyātmakasya tu pādasya svarūpārthāviśeṣe tātparyabhedena punaruktau pādābhyāsaparipāṭyā svatantrapadāśrayo lāṭānuprāso bhavati /
pādābhyāsakrameṇa ceti kramagrahaṇena sakṛddvistriśca pādābhyāse ye bhedāḥ saṃbhavanti tatsvīkāreṇa pādābhyāse lāṭānuprāsasya pravṛttiḥ sūcitā /
tasyodāharaṇam----
children.translated_text: But when a verse-quarter, consisting of a collection of words, has repetition due to a difference in purport despite no difference in form and meaning, the <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s> based on independent words occurs in the sequence of <s>pāda</s>-repetition. By the word 'sequence' in 'by the sequence of <s>pāda</s>-repetition,' it is indicated that the <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s> operates in <s>pāda</s>-repetition through the acceptance of the distinctions that arise in repetition occurring once, twice, or thrice. An example of that:

children.text: striyo mahati bhartṛbhya āgasyapi na cukrudhuḥ /
children.translated_text: The wives did not become angry with their husbands even for a great offense;

children.text: bhartāro 'pi sati strībhya āgasyapi na cukrudhuḥ // UKss_1.*7 //
children.translated_text: the husbands too did not become angry with their wives even for an offense. [UKss 1.*7]

children.text:
mahatyapyāgasīti saṃbandhaḥ /
tathā ca satyapyāgasīti bhartṛbhya iti strībhya iti ca 'krudha druhe'ti saṃpradānatā /
atra ekatra pāde nāyakagatāparādhaviṣayatvena strīkartṛkaḥ krodhābhāvaḥ pratipāditaḥ /
aparatra tu nāyikānāṃ yo bhartṛpraṇayātikramātmako 'parādhastadviṣayo nāyakakartṛkaḥ krodhābhāvobhihitaḥ /
atastātparyabhedaḥ svarūpārthāviśeṣaśca /
padasamudāyātmakasya ca pādasyābhyāsaḥ /
evamayaṃ svatantrapadāśrayo lāṭānuprāso dvividho 'bhihitaḥ /
ekaikapadāśrayaḥ padasamudāyāśrayaśca svatantrapadāśrayo lāṭānuprāsaḥ /
children.translated_text: The connection is: 'even for a great offense.' And likewise: 'even though there was an offense.' 'With husbands' and 'with wives' take the dative case, following the rule '<s>krudha druhe</s> [take the dative].' Here, in one verse-quarter, the absence of anger on the part of the wives is presented, with respect to offenses committed by the heroes. In the other [quarter], the absence of anger on the part of the heroes is stated, with respect to offenses in the form of transgressions of the heroines' love. Thus there is a difference in purport and no difference in form and meaning. And there is repetition of the verse-quarter consisting of a collection of words. Thus this <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s> based on independent words has been described as twofold: the <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s> based on individual words and that based on a collection of words constituting a verse-quarter.

children.text:
dvayoranupalabhyamānasuptiḍoḥ paratantrayoḥ śabdayoryo lāṭānuprāsastasyāpi dvaividhyaṃ, padadvitayāśrayatvena ekapadādhāratvena ca /
taduktam----
'sa padadvitayasthityā dvayoḥ'iti /
so 'nekadhā bhedairbhidyate iti saṃbandhaḥ /
tathā dvayorvaikapadāśrayāditi /
children.translated_text: The <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s> of two dependent words, i.e., words without perceptible nominal or verbal endings, is also twofold — based on a pair of words and based on a single word. This was stated: 'That, by the occurrence of a pair of words, of two' — and the connection is: 'it is divided in many ways by distinctions.' And: 'because of one word being the basis for both.'
An example of the former:
Somewhere with fully bloomed lotuses, with bees deluded by lotuses,
loud with the humming of bees, [and] full of abundant <s>sārasas</s> (cranes). [UKss 1.*8]

children.text:
sārasāḥ lakṣmaṇākhyāḥ pakṣiviśeṣāḥ /
atra kamalaṣaṭpadamukharaśabdānāṃ svarūpārthabhede 'pi tātparyabhedena punaruktiḥ padadvitayāśrayitvaṃ ca /
tātparyabhedaścātra kamalaṣaṭpadaśabdayoḥ kārakaśaktibhedāt /
tathāhi /
pūrvaḥ kamalaśabdo 'tra vikāsakriyākartṛtvaparatayopāttaḥ, uttarastu bhramaṇakriyākartṛbhūtaṣaṭpadādhāratvena /
tathā pūrvaḥ ṣaṭpadaśabdo bhramaṇakriyāṃ prati kartṛtvenopavarṇitaḥ, uttarastu kvāṇakriyāsaṃbandhitvena /
mukharaśabdau tu
children.translated_text: <s>Sārasāḥ</s> are a particular kind of birds called <s>lakṣmaṇa</s>. Here, although the words <s>kamala</s>, <s>ṣaṭpada</s>, and <s>mukhara</s> differ in form and meaning, there is repetition due to a difference in purport, and each is based on a pair of words. The difference in purport here for the words <s>kamala</s> and <s>ṣaṭpada</s> is due to the difference in their case-role capacity. For the first word <s>kamala</s> (lotus) here is taken in the sense of being the agent of the action of blooming, while the second is [taken] as the substrate for the bees (<s>ṣaṭpada</s>) that are the agents of the action of hovering. Likewise, the first word <s>ṣaṭpada</s> (bee) is described as agent with respect to the action of hovering, while the second is [taken] in relation to the action of humming. The two words <s>mukhara</s> (loud, resonant),
being qualifiers,

children.text:
saśabdatvaṃ bhinnārthaniṣṭhatayāvagamayataḥ /
tathāhi /
pūrveṇa mukharaśabdena śaranniṣṭhaṃ maukharyamavagamyate, apareṇa tu sārasaniṣṭham /
evamayaṃ padadvitayaparatantraśabdadvayāśrayo lāṭānuprāso 'bhihitaḥ /
children.translated_text: convey the quality of being sonorous as pertaining to different referents. For by the first word <s>mukhara</s>, the resonance pertaining to autumn is conveyed, while by the second, that pertaining to the <s>sārasas</s> (cranes). Thus this <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s> based on a pair of dependent words has been described.
The [lāṭānuprāsa] based on a pair of words occurring within a single word-unit is described by 'because of one word being the basis for both.' An example of that:
Having defeated the stamens of the freshly-blossomed [lotuses], adorned with rows of filaments,
the pale blue lotus attained the status of an ear-ornament on the moon-[faces] of women. [UKss 1.*9]

children.text:
atra nārīmukheṣviti vadanānāṃ candreṇopamitatvādasitotpalasya śaśakarūpatā dhvanyate /
kiñjalkaśabdayoścātra svarūpārthābheda ekapadāśrayatvaṃ tātparyabhedaśca /
ekasya jīyamānatayā upādānāt, aparasya jayanakriyākartṛbhūtāyāsau śreṇistatsaṃbandhitvena /
evamayaṃ paratantrayoḥ śabdayorlāṭānuprāso dvividho nirūpitaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, by 'on the moon-faces of women,' since the faces are compared to the moon, the pale blue lotus (<s>asitotpala</s>) suggests its resemblance to the mark of the hare on the moon. And here the two words <s>kiñjalka</s> (filament) have no difference in form and meaning, are based on a single word-unit, and differ in purport — one being taken as that which is defeated, and the other as the row [of filaments] belonging to the agent of the action of defeating, by relation to that [row]. Thus this <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s> of two dependent words has been determined as twofold.

children.text:
svatantraparatantrayostu yatraikasya śabdasya padāntarānupraveśaḥ, aparasya tu svātantryeṇa padarūpatayāvasthānaṃ tatra bhavati /
taduktam---'ekasya pūrvavattadanyasya svatantratvāt'iti /
ekasya pūrvavatpadāntarāśrayeṇāvasthānādityarthaḥ /
tasyodāharaṇam---
children.translated_text: As for [the combination of] one independent and one dependent — where one word enters into another word [as a component], while the other stands independently in the form of a word — that [lāṭānuprāsa] occurs there. This was stated: 'of one, as before, because of the independence of the other.' The meaning is: because of one's position as dependent on another word, as before. An example of that:
Having come from <s>Mānasa</s> [lake] with intense longing for the <s>padminī</s> (lotus-pond),
the <s>haṃsas</s> (swans) bared their teeth, as it were, at the <s>padminī</s> (lotus-pond) from the <s>haṃsa</s>-colony. [UKss 1.*10]

children.text:
mānasāt saroviśeṣāt /
danturayāmāsuḥ mahattvācchuklatvācca unnatadantā iva cakruḥ /
atra svarūpārthāphabhede 'pi padminīśabdayorhaṃsaśabdayośca tātparyabedātpunaruktiḥ /

children.translated_text: One [<s>padminī</s>] enters into another word [as a component], while the other serves the purpose of indicating the object of desire.

children.text: tathā ekasya haṃsaśabdasya danturaṇakriyākartṛbhūtārthābhidhāyitvāt, aparasya tu kulasaṃbandhitvāt /
children.translated_text: Likewise, one word <s>haṃsa</s> denotes the meaning of being the agent of the action of baring teeth, while the other is [taken] in relation to the flock (<s>kula</s>).
Thus this fivefold <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s> has been demonstrated.

children.text: svatantraparatantrāṇāṃ tasya pratyekaṃ dvibhedatvāt svatantrapara tantrayośca samuditayorekaprakāratvāt //
children.translated_text: Because the [lāṭānuprāsa] of independent and dependent [words] each has two varieties, and because the combination of independent and dependent together has one variety.

From <s>Mānasa</s>, a particular lake. <s>Danturayāmāsuḥ</s> means they appeared as if with raised teeth, due to their greatness and whiteness. Here, despite no difference in form and meaning, there is repetition of the words <s>padminī</s> and <s>haṃsa</s> due to a difference in purport.
<s>Rūpaka</s> (metaphor):
When, due to the absence of connection through direct denotation, one word

children.text: guṇavṛtti pradhānena yujyate rūpakaṃ tu tat // UKss_1.11 //
children.translated_text: functions as a qualifier for another word and is identified with the principal — that is <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor). [UKss 1.11]

children.text: bandhastasya yataḥ śrutyā śrutyarthābhyāṃ ca tena tat /
children.translated_text: Since its binding is through direct denotation, or through both denotation and meaning, therefore it
encompasses an entire object, or operates upon only a part. [UKss 1.12]
That which encompasses an entire object is called <s>mālā-rūpaka</s> (garland-metaphor).
That which operates upon only a part, through the figuration by another's form — [UKss 1.13]

children.text:
padāntarasya guṇavṛtterapareṇa padena yoge rūpakaṃ bhavati /
nanvevaṃ sati nīlamutpalamityatrāpi nīlaśabdasya guṇavṛtterutpalaśabdena yoge rūpakatāprasaṅga ityāśaṅkyoktaṃ---śrutyā saṃbandhavirahāditi /
śrutirnirantarārthaniṣṭhaḥ śabdavyāpāraḥ /
tayā śrutyā anupapadyamānapadāntarasaṃbandhaṃ sat padāntaraṃ guṇavṛtti yatrāpareṇa padena yujyate tatra rūpakatā /
yathā----
children.translated_text: When a word functioning as a qualifier for another word is combined with another word, <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) occurs. Now, if this were so, then even in 'a blue lotus' (<s>nīlam utpalam</s>), the word <s>nīla</s> (blue), functioning as a qualifier, when combined with the word <s>utpala</s> (lotus), would absurdly result in metaphor — anticipating this objection, it is said: 'due to the absence of connection through direct denotation.' <s>Śruti</s> (direct denotation) is the verbal operation directed toward the immediate meaning. When a word functioning as a qualifier for another word — [a qualifier] whose connection with that other word cannot be established through direct denotation — is combined with another word, there is metaphor. For example:
With a water-pot of the moon made of moonlight-water, strewn with star-flowers,
the maiden Night gradually watered the garden of the sky. [UKss 1.*11]
Thus.

children.text:
atrāmbuśabdo nirantarārthaniṣṭhaśabdavyāpāragocarīkṛte udakatve vartamāno jyotsnāśabdena sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ nānubhavati /
ambutvajyotsnātvayorekārthasamavāyābhāvāt /
ato 'mbugatāḥ śauklyāhlādakatvaprasaraṇaśīlatvādayo ye guṇāstatsadṛśajyotsnāgataguṇavṛttiḥ sannambuśabdo jyotsnāyāṃ vartate /
tenāmbuśabdasya śrutyā nirantarārthaniṣṭhena abhidhāvyāpāreṇa yaḥ padāntareṇa jyotsnāśabdena saṃbandhastacchūnyatvādguṇavṛttitā /
ato 'tra
children.translated_text: Here the word <s>ambu</s> (water), which in the domain of verbal operation directed toward the immediate meaning refers to water, does not experience co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) with the word <s>jyotsnā</s> (moonlight) — because there is no co-occurrence of water-ness and moonlight-ness in a single referent. Therefore the word <s>ambu</s>, functioning as a qualifier by virtue of qualities such as whiteness, capacity to delight, and the tendency to spread — which are shared with moonlight possessing similar qualities — applies to moonlight. Thus the word <s>ambu</s>, because it lacks the connection with the other word <s>jyotsnā</s> through direct denotation (i.e., the verbal operation directed toward the immediate meaning), has the status of functioning as a qualifier. Therefore here

children.text:
rūpakatā /
nacaivaṃ nīlamutpalamityādau śrutyā saṃbandhavirahādguṇavṛttitvaṃ, kiṃtarhi svata eveti na rūpakatāprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: there is metaphor. And in 'a blue lotus' (<s>nīlam utpalam</s>) and the like, the qualifier-status is not due to the absence of connection through direct denotation, but rather is inherent — therefore there is no absurd consequence of metaphor.

children.text:
nanu viruddhārthābhidhāyinoḥ samānādhikaraṇayoḥ śabdayornirantarārthaniṣṭhena abhidhāvyāpāreṇa anupapdyamānānyonyasamanvayatvādyadyekasya lakṣaṇayā guṇavṛttitvamabhidhīyate, evaṃ sati paryāyeṇātra guṇavṛttitvaṃ prāpnoti /
niyamakaraṇābhāvāt /
tataśca yathāmbuśabdasya jyotsnāśabdasāmānādhikaraṇyādguṇavṛttitvamuktaṃ, tadvajjyotsnāśabdasyāpi ambuśabdasāmānādhikaraṇyādguṇavṛttitvaṃ kathaṃ na syādityāśaṅkyoktaṃ pradhāneneti /
pradhānārthānurodhena upasarjanasya lakṣaṇayā guṇavṛttitvamupapannam /
pradhānavaśavartitvādguṇānāmityabhiprāyaḥ /
ataśca prākaraṇikārthābhidhāyitvātpradhānārthaviṣayo yo jyotsnāśabdaḥ tadanurodhena ambuśabdasya aprākaraṇikārthatvādapradhānārthasya guṇavṛttitvamupapannamiti na paryāyeṇa jyotsnāmbuśabdayoḥ parasparānurodhena guṇavṛttitpaprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: Now, [objection:] when two words with contradictory meanings are in co-referential position (<s>samānādhikaraṇa</s>), since their mutual connection is impossible through the expressive function (<s>abhidhāvyāpāra</s>) that culminates in uninterrupted meaning, if the secondary usage (<s>guṇavṛttitva</s>) of one is stated through figurative indication (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>), then by alternation, secondary usage would obtain here [for the other word as well], because there is no rule restricting [it to one]. Therefore, just as the secondary usage of the word 'water' (<s>ambu</s>) was stated due to its co-referential position with the word 'moonlight' (<s>jyotsnā</s>), why should there not be secondary usage of the word 'moonlight' as well, due to its co-referential position with the word 'water'? — Anticipating this [objection], it was said 'by [following] the principal [meaning]' (<s>pradhānena</s>). The secondary usage of the subordinate (<s>upasarjana</s>) through figurative indication is established by conformity with the principal meaning. The intended sense is: because secondary elements (<s>guṇa</s>) are subservient to the principal. Therefore, the word 'moonlight,' which denotes the principal meaning because it expresses the contextually relevant meaning (<s>prākaraṇikārtha</s>), is followed; and by conformity with it, the secondary usage of the word 'water,' which denotes the non-principal meaning because it expresses what is not contextually relevant, is established. Thus there is no absurd consequence of mutual secondary usage of the words 'moonlight' and 'water' through mutual conformity by alternation.

children.text:
nanu ca jyotsnāmbunetyatra ambunaḥ prādhānyaṃ jyotsnāyāśca guṇabhāvaḥ /
tathā hi /
etasmiñśloke tadbhāvādhyavasānena sekāvacchāditarūpatayā sekātmakatvena yāsau vyomno vyāptirasicyateti pratipāditā, tayā svasādhanabhūtaṃ yattadambho 'pekṣitaṃ tadatra jyotsnayā viśiṣyate jyotsnaivāmbviti /
yadatra sekasādhanatvenāmbu apekṣitaṃ tajjyotsnaivetyarthaḥ /
uktaṃ ca "upasarjanopameyaṃ kṛtvā tu samāsametayorubhayoḥ /
yacca prayucyate tadrūpakamanyatsamāsoktam"iti /
etayorubhayoriti /
upamānopameyayorityarthaḥ /
tatkathamidamuktaṃ jyotsnāpadasya prādhānyāttadvaśenāmbuśabdasya guṇavṛttitvaṃ kalpyate iti /
ucyate /
atra khalu dve 'vasthe vidyete /
ekā tāvajjyotsnāyā ambūkaraṇāvasthā /
aparā tu ambutvamāpāditāyā jyotsnāyāḥ sekasaṃbandharūpā /
tatra yadā tāvajjyotsnā amburūpatvamāpadyate tadā prākaraṇikatvāt jyotsnā pradhānam /
ambu ca tadviparyayādguṇaḥ /
tadānīṃ cāmbuśabdo jyotsnāśabdānurodhenāmbugataśauklyādiguṇasadṛśaguṇayogāllakṣaṇayā jyotsnāyāṃ vṛttimanubhavati /
tadā ca tasya pradhānārthānurodhādguṇavṛttitvena rūpakatvamuktam /
yadā tvasau ambuśabda āpāditāmbubhāvajyotsnābhidhāyī san sekakriyayā samanvayamāpadyamāno yadetadatra sekasādhanatvenāmbu upayujyate tajjyotsnaiveti jyotsnayā viśiṣyate tadā tasya na rūpakāvasthā /
pūrvāvasthāyāmevānubhūtaguṇavṛttitvāt /
atastasyāmavasthāyāmasau atiśayokticchāyāṃ bhajate /
pūrvāvasthāpekṣayātvetadrūpakamuktam /
pradhānānurodhena tatra guṇeṣu vartamānatvāt /
rūpakatvaṃ cātrādhyāropyamāṇagatena rūpeṇa adhyāropaviṣayasya vastuno rūpavataḥ kriyamāṇatvādanvarthaṃ draṣṭavyam /
children.translated_text: Now, [objection:] in 'with moonlight-water' (<s>jyotsnāmbunā</s>), 'water' is the principal and 'moonlight' has the status of a secondary element. This is so [because:] In this verse, through the determination of identity with that [water], the pervading of the sky was presented as having the form of sprinkling — with the appearance of being covered by sprinkling, as being of the nature of sprinkling, 'it was sprinkled' — and by this [act of sprinkling], water, which is the instrument for its accomplishment, was required; that [water] is here qualified by moonlight [as] 'moonlight is itself the water.' The meaning is: the water that is required here as the instrument of sprinkling is nothing but moonlight. And it has been said: 'But when a compound is made of both, making the subordinate element the object of comparison (<s>upameya</s>), what is employed is <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor); otherwise it is <s>samāsokti</s> (compound expression).' 'Of both' means: of the standard of comparison (<s>upamāna</s>) and the object of comparison (<s>upameya</s>). Then how is it said that because of the primacy of the word 'moonlight,' the secondary usage of the word 'water' is conceived by its force? [Answer:] Here indeed there are two stages. The first is the stage of moonlight being made into water. The second is the form of the relation of sprinkling, belonging to moonlight that has been made to assume the nature of water. Now, when moonlight takes on the form of water, then moonlight is the principal, being contextually relevant, and water is the secondary, being the opposite thereof. At that time, the word 'water,' by conformity with the word 'moonlight,' through the connection with qualities resembling the qualities of whiteness etc. belonging to water, undergoes application to moonlight through figurative indication (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>). And at that time, its metaphorical nature (<s>rūpakatva</s>) is stated as secondary usage by conformity with the principal meaning. But when that word 'water,' denoting moonlight that has been made to assume the nature of water, comes into connection with the action of sprinkling — [namely] 'the water that is employed here as the instrument of sprinkling is nothing but moonlight' — and is qualified by moonlight, then its state is not that of <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor), because its secondary usage was already experienced in the prior stage. Therefore, in that [second] stage, it partakes of the semblance of <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole). However, with reference to the prior stage, this is called <s>rūpaka</s>, because of operating in the secondary [sense] by conformity with the principal. And the metaphorical nature (<s>rūpakatva</s>) here should be seen as literal: because the form belonging to what is superimposed is made to belong to the object that is the locus of superimposition, which possesses [its own] form.

children.text:
atra copamānavartino ye guṇāstatsadṛśaguṇadarśanādupameya upamānagatayoḥ śabdarūpayorāropaḥ /
tatra trayo darśanabhedāḥ /
kecidatra śabdāropapūrvakamarthāropaṃ bruvate, apare tvarthāropapūrvakaṃ śabdāropam /
anyaistu śabdāropārthāropayoryaugapadyamabhidhīyate /
ayameva ca pakṣo yukta iva dṛśyate /
tadāhuḥ---
children.translated_text: And here, because of perceiving qualities in the object of comparison that are similar to the qualities present in the standard of comparison, there is superimposition of both the word-form and meaning-form belonging to the standard upon the object of comparison. Therein there are three views regarding the distinction. Some here state that meaning-superimposition follows upon word-superimposition; others, that word-superimposition follows upon meaning-superimposition. Yet others hold that word-superimposition and meaning-superimposition are simultaneous. And this very view appears to be correct. Thus they say:
"Some say that in <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor), the identity of form [arises] from figurative transfer of the word;
others say the word-superimposition here [arises] from superimposition of identity of form.
For those who perceive qualities in the object of comparison that are equal to the qualities of the standard of comparison,
the word-form and meaning-form of that [standard] flash simultaneously upon the object of comparison."
Thus.

children.text:
tatreti /
upameye ityarthaḥ /
tacchabdarūpateti /
upamānaśabdāropa upamānarūpāropaśca /
children.translated_text: 'There' means: in the object of comparison (<s>upameya</s>). 'The word-form and meaning-form of that' means: the superimposition of the word of the standard of comparison (<s>upamāna</s>) and the superimposition of the form of the standard.

children.text:
tasya ca rūpakasya dviprakāratā /
svakaṇṭhena sakalarūpaṇābhidhānādekaḥ prakāraḥ /
taduktm---"bandhastasya yataḥ śrutyā tena tatsamastavastuviṣayam"iti /
śrutirnirantarārthaniṣṭho 'bhidhāvyāpārastasyodāharaṇaṃ 'jyotsnāmbunā'ityādyuktam /
śāritaṃ śabalitam /
atra hi sarveṣāmeva rūpyatvenopāttānāṃ jyotsnendutārārātrivyomnāṃ yathākramamambukumbhakusumakanyodyānāni rūpakatvena svakaṇṭhenopāttāni, na tvarthākṣiptaṃ kasyacidrūpaṇam /
tena śrutyaivātra rūpaṇā /
ataḥ samastavastuviṣayatvam /
samagrāṇi hyatra rūpyatvenābhimatāni vastūni svakaṇṭhenopāttasya rūpakasya viṣayaḥ /
ayamasāvekaḥ prakāraḥ /
children.translated_text: And that <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) is of two kinds. One kind is where the entire metaphorical identification is expressed in one's own voice (<s>svakaṇṭha</s>). As stated: 'Since its composition is through direct expression (<s>śruti</s>), therefore it pertains to the complete object.' Direct expression (<s>śruti</s>) is the expressive function that culminates in uninterrupted meaning. Its example is 'with moonlight-water' and so on, as mentioned. <s>Śāritam</s> means 'variegated.' For here, all those taken as objects of metaphorical identification — moonlight, moon, stars, night, and sky — are respectively presented in one's own voice as water, pot, flower, maiden, and garden as <s>rūpaka</s>; no metaphorical identification of any is merely implied by the meaning. Therefore the metaphorical identification here is through direct expression alone. Hence it pertains to the complete object. For all the things intended as objects of metaphorical identification are the domain of the <s>rūpaka</s> presented in one's own voice. This is the first kind.

children.text:
yatra tu kiṃcitsvakaṇṭhena kiṃciccārthādraṣaṇaṃ bhavati, tatra śrutyarthābhyāṃ rūpaṇādaparaḥ prakāro bhavati /
tatra caikadeśavivartitvam, ekadeśaviśeṣeṇa
children.translated_text: But where some metaphorical identification is in one's own voice and some is through the implied meaning, there, because the identification is through both direct expression and meaning, another kind arises. And therein there is <s>ekadeśavivartitvam</s> (partial variation), because of operating with a distinction in one part —

children.text:
svakaṇṭhoktyā vartanāt /
taduktaṃ 'yataśca śrutyarthābhyāṃ tasya bandhastena tadekadeśavivarti ca'iti /
tasyodāharaṇam----
children.translated_text: because of operating through one's own stated expression. As stated: 'And since its composition is through both direct expression and meaning, therefore it is partially varying' (<s>ekadeśavivarti</s>). Its example:
With their tail-feather fans like young rice-shoots, rising and falling,
the royal swans fanned the lake-kings — [it was] autumn herself [who did it].

children.text:
picchālyaḥ pakṣapaṅktayaḥ /
rājahaṃsā raktacañcupādā haṃsāḥ /
avījyanteti /
vījirdhātuṣvapaṭhito 'pi śiṣṭhaprayogāt milikhaciklavikṣapivaddhā tutayā draṣṭavyaḥ /
atra dve rūpaṇe svakaṇṭhenābhihite picchālībālaśālibhiriti saronṛpā iti ca /
tathā hi ekatra picchālyo bālarūpatvena rūpitāḥ, aparatra tu sarāṃsi nṛparūpatvena /
rājahaṃsānāṃ cāmararūpatvena rūpaṇā arthākṣiptā, śaradaśca prakṛtāyā nāyikātvena /
śarannāyikayā kartṛbhūtayā rājahaṃsacāmaraiḥ picchālībālaśālibhiḥ saronṛpā vījyante smeti hyatra vākyārthaḥ /
evametau rūpakasya samastavastuviṣayaikadeśavivartilakṣaṇau dvau prakārāvuktau /
yadi vā mālārūpakasya samastavastuviṣayatā tatra hyekasmin rūpye samuccayena asyante kṣipyante bahūni rūpakāṇi /
taduktaṃ ----
'samastavastuviṣayaṃ mālārūpakamucyate /
'yadveti prakārāntaropakṣepārthaḥ /
tasyodāharaṇam---
children.translated_text: <s>Picchālīs</s> are rows of tail-feathers. <s>Rājahaṃsas</s> are swans with red beaks and feet. 'Fanned' (<s>avījyanta</s>): though the root <s>vīji</s> is not listed in the <s>dhātupāṭha</s>, it should be understood as accepted on the basis of learned usage, like [the roots] <s>milikha</s>, <s>cikla</s>, <s>vikṣapi</s>, and <s>vaddhā</s>, by analogy. Here two metaphorical identifications are expressed in one's own voice: 'with tail-feather fans like young rice-shoots' and 'lake-kings.' Thus, in one case the tail-feathers are identified as fans (<s>bāla</s>/young shoots), and in the other the lakes are identified as kings. The identification of the royal swans as <s>cāmaras</s> (fly-whisks) is implied by the meaning, and that of autumn — being the subject — as the heroine (<s>nāyikā</s>). The sentence-meaning here is: autumn as the heroine, the agent, fans the lake-kings with the royal-swan fly-whisks that are the tail-feather fans like young rice-shoots. Thus these two types of <s>rūpaka</s> — characterized by complete object-domain and partial variation — have been described. Alternatively, <s>mālā-rūpaka</s> (garland metaphor) has the complete object-domain, for in it many metaphors are cast together in succession upon a single object of identification. As stated: 'What pertains to the complete object is called <s>mālā-rūpaka</s> (garland metaphor).' 'Or' (<s>yadvā</s>) is for introducing an alternative type. Its example:
The braids of forest-corner goddesses, the chains of death for women of travelers,
the sword-creepers of <s>Māra</s>'s heroes — the rows of bees shone forth.

children.text:
vanāntā vanaikadeśaḥ /
veṇyaḥ keśapāśāḥ /
kālaśṛṅkhalā antakaprayuktā ākarṣaṇaśṛṅkhalāḥ /
mārapravīrā manmathasaṃbandhino bhaṭāḥ /
atra bhṛṅgamālānāmeva kevalānāṃ rūpyatvenopāttānāṃ tisro rūpaṇāḥ kṛtāḥ vanāntadevatāveṇya ityevamādinā /
tenātra samastavastuviṣayatā, ekasmin rūpye samuccayena bahūnāṃ rūpaṇānāṃ kṣiptatvāt-----
children.translated_text: <s>Vanānta</s> means a part of the forest. <s>Veṇīs</s> are braids of hair. <s>Kālaśṛṅkhalās</s> are chains of death, i.e., chains of dragging employed by <s>Antaka</s> (Death). <s>Mārapravīras</s> are warriors associated with <s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love). Here, for the rows of bees alone, taken as the single object of metaphorical identification, three identifications are made — as 'braids of forest-corner goddesses' and so on. Therefore here there is the complete object-domain, because many identifications are cast together in succession upon a single object of identification.

children.text:
ekadeśavivarti tu pararūpeṇa rūpaṇādbhavati /
taduktaṃ 'ekadeśavṛtti syātpararūpema rūpaṇāt'iti /
tasyodāharaṇam /
children.translated_text: The partially varying [type], however, arises from identification through another form. As stated: 'The partially occurring [type] arises from identification through another form.' Its example:
With the arrows of rain-shower streams, shining in the expanse of the sky,
the white clouds adorned the kingdom of the directions.

children.text:
āsāro vegavadvarṣam /
viśikhāḥ śarāḥ /
atra prasādhyata ityayaṃ śabdaḥ śleṣacchāyayā dvayorarthayorvartate bhūṣaṇe upārjane ca /
tatra bhūṣaṇaṃ prakṛtam /
śaratsamayo hyatra prastutaḥ /
tatra ca śuklairbalāhakairdiśo bhūṣyante /
yadupārjanaṃ tadaprakṛtatvādatra paramanyat /
tasya ca parasyāprakṛtasya upārjanasya yattadrūpaṃ kārakakadambakaṃ yena tadrūpavatktrayate nṛpaviśikharājyasaṃgrāmabhūmyātmakaṃ tenātra yathākramaṃ balāhakāsāradhārādiṅabhobhāgānāṃ rūpyatvenābhimatānāṃ rūpaṇā vihitā /
tenātraikadeśavṛttitvam /
ekadeśavṛttītyatra hi ekadā andā īśaḥ prabhaviṣṇuryo vākyārthastadvṛttatvaṃ rūpakasyābhimatam /
viśeṣoktilakṣaṇe ca bhāmahavivaraṇe bhaṭṭodbhaṭena ekadeśaśabda evaṃ vyākhyāto yathohāsmābhirnirūpitaḥ tatra viśeṣoktilakṣaṇam----

children.translated_text: "When, upon the departure of one element, there is praise of another quality —
that is known as <s>viśeṣokti</s> (specific statement), serving to display distinction. Thus:"

children.text: tenātra viśeṣoktilakṣaṇavadekadeśaśabdena anyadā prabhaviṣṇurvākyārtha ucyate, anyatra ca anyadā prabhaviṣṇūpārjanam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, here just as in the definition of <s>viśeṣokti</s>, by the word <s>ekadeśa</s> is meant 'the predominant sentence-meaning' in one context, and 'the predominant conquest' in another.

children.text: aprakṛtaṃ hi tat śleṣavaśenātra nītaṃ, tenātraikadeśavṛttitā //
children.translated_text: For that [conquest] is contextually irrelevant and is introduced here by the force of <s>śleṣa</s> (double entendre); therefore here there is partial occurrence.

<s>Āsāra</s> means forceful rain. <s>Viśikhas</s> are arrows. Here the word 'adorned' (<s>prasādhyate</s>) operates in two meanings through the semblance of <s>śleṣa</s> (double entendre): ornamentation and conquest. Therein, ornamentation is the contextually relevant meaning, for the autumn season is the subject here; and in that context, the directions are adorned by white clouds. Conquest, being contextually irrelevant, is the other, secondary [meaning]. And the form of that other, contextually irrelevant conquest — [namely] the group of agents and instruments by which it is made to possess that form — consisting of king, arrows, kingdom, and battlefield — by this, the identifications of clouds, rain-shower streams, the sky-expanse, and the directions, which are taken as the objects of metaphorical identification, are respectively established. Therefore here there is partial occurrence (<s>ekadeśavṛttitva</s>). In 'partially occurring' (<s>ekadeśavṛtti</s>), the 'one portion' (<s>ekadeśa</s>) refers to 'the sentence-meaning that is the predominant master,' and the <s>rūpaka</s>'s occurrence in that is what is intended. And in the definition of <s>viśeṣokti</s> (specific statement) in the commentary on <s>Bhāmaha</s>, <s>Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa</s> explained the word <s>ekadeśa</s> in the same way as we have analyzed it. There the definition of <s>viśeṣokti</s> is:
<s>Dīpaka</s> (illumination):
Pertaining to the beginning, middle, or end; connected with what is principal and what is secondary;
where properties containing an implicit comparison are incorporated — that the learned know as <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination).

children.text:
yatrāntargator'thasāmarthyāvaseyatvādupamānopameyabhāvo yeṣāṃ tathāvidhānāṃ dharmaṇāmupanibandhastatra kāvyadīpakaṃ bhavati /
tathāvidhakāvyaviṣayatvācca dīpakasya tatkāvyaṃ dīpakamityupacārātsāmānādhikaraṇyam /
atra ca dharmāṇāmekavāramupanibandho draṣṭavyaḥ /
asakṛdupādāne hi teṣāṃ prativastūpamāṃ vakṣyati /
ata eva caikadeśavartināmapi teṣāṃ dharmāṇāṃ yau dvau upamānopameyabhāvena avasthitau vākyārthau bahabo vā tathāvidhāstaduddīpanahetutvāddīpakatā /
yāvacca teṣāṃ dharmāṇāmupamānopameyabhāvasamanvayenātropanibandhastāvadbalātprādhānyetarayogitvamāpatati /
upameyasya /
prākaraṇikatayā prādhānyādupamānasya ca tādarthyena
children.translated_text: Where properties whose relation of standard-and-object-of-comparison is to be inferred from the force of the meaning are incorporated as implicit comparisons (<s>antargatopamā</s>) — there is poetic <s>dīpaka</s>. And because of being the subject-matter of such poetry, the poem [itself] is called <s>dīpaka</s> by figurative transfer, through co-referential usage. Here, the incorporation of the properties should be understood as occurring once only. For if they were taken up more than once, that would constitute <s>prativastūpamā</s> (counterpart simile), which will be discussed later. Therefore, even when those properties occupy only one part, the two sentence-meanings — or many such — that stand in the relation of standard and object of comparison, illuminate [each other]; and it is because of being the cause of that illumination that [the figure is called] <s>dīpaka</s>. And insofar as those properties are incorporated here through the connection of standard-and-object-of-comparison relation, the connection with principal and secondary forcefully obtains —

children.text:
guṇabhāvāt /
evaṃ ca prādhānyetarayogina ityayamatrānuvādaḥ /
prāptārthatvāt /
prādhānyaṃ ca itaraccāprādhānyam /
tābhyāṃ yogaḥ saṃbandho vidyate yeṣāṃ te tathoktāḥ /
children.translated_text: because of the secondary status of the object of comparison (<s>upameya</s>), which has primacy due to its contextual relevance, and because of the secondary nature (<s>guṇabhāva</s>) of the standard of comparison due to its being for the purpose of [illustrating] the former. Thus, 'connected with what is principal and what is secondary' is here a restatement [of what is already entailed], since its meaning is already obtained. 'Principal' and 'other' [means] 'non-principal'; connection (<s>yoga</s>) means relation with those two — those that have [this relation] are so called.

children.text:
asya ca dīpakasya traividhyam, teṣāṃ dharmāṇāmādimadhyāntavākyaviṣayatvenopanibandhāt /
taduktam 'ādimadhyāntaviṣayāḥ'iti /
children.translated_text: And this <s>dīpaka</s> is of three kinds, because those properties are incorporated as pertaining to sentences at the beginning, middle, or end. As stated: 'pertaining to the beginning, middle, or end.'
Example of <s>ādi-dīpaka</s> (illumination at the beginning):
The autumn season gathered up the beauty of <s>kadamba</s> flowers
and the entire store of happiness of women separated from their beloveds.

children.text:
atra saṃharaṇātmā dharmaḥ kadambakusumaśobhākarmakatvena virahiṇīsukhasampatkarmakatvena ca upanibadhyamāno 'ntargatopamaḥ /
śaratsamayasyopavarṇyamānatayā kadambakusumaśrīsaṃharasya prākaraṇikārthaniṣṭhatvādivrahiṇīsukhasaṃpatsaṃhārasya cāprākaraṇikārthaviṣayatvāt /
tenātrāntargatopamatvam, yathā preyoviyoginīnāṃ niḥśeṣāḥ sukhasampadaḥ saṃjahāra tathā kadambakusumaśriyo 'pīti /
śaratkālaśabdasya cātra śaratsamayaḥ śleṣacchāyayā antakānurañcito vācyaḥ /
saṃhārasyāntakakarmatvāt /
atra ca prathama eva vākye saṃjahāretyasyopanibaddhasya dvitīyavākye anuṣaṅgacchāyayā upajīvyamānatvādādidīpakatvam /
children.translated_text: Here the property consisting of gathering (<s>saṃharaṇa</s>), being incorporated with the beauty of <s>kadamba</s> flowers as its object and also with the happiness of women separated from their beloveds as its object, contains an implicit comparison. Since the autumn season is being described, the gathering of the beauty of <s>kadamba</s> flowers pertains to the contextually relevant meaning, while the gathering of the happiness of women separated from their beloveds pertains to the contextually irrelevant meaning. Therefore here there is implicit comparison: just as [autumn] gathered up the entire store of happiness of women separated from their beloveds, so too [it gathered] the beauty of <s>kadamba</s> flowers. And the word 'autumn season' (<s>śaratkāla</s>) here should be understood, through the semblance of <s>śleṣa</s>, as tinged with [the meaning of] <s>Antaka</s> (Death), because gathering is the action of Death. And here, because [the property] 'gathered' (<s>saṃjahāra</s>), incorporated in the first sentence, is drawn upon in the second sentence through the semblance of syntactic continuation (<s>anuṣaṅga</s>), it is <s>ādi-dīpaka</s> (illumination at the beginning).
Example of <s>madhya-dīpaka</s> (illumination in the middle):
Dwelling in foreign lands, the sight of women whose husbands have departed —
only for suffering did that autumn exist, for those away from home.

children.text:
yātapatikāḥ proṣitabhartṛkāḥ /
śaradaḥ prākaraṇikatvādvideśavasatiyātapatikājanadarśanayoścāprākaraṇikatvādatrāntargatopamatā /
atra ca yātapatikājanadarśanaṃ duḥkhāya kevalamabhūditi madhyame vākye pravāsiduḥ khaikahetutvalakṣaṇo dharma upāttaḥ sannādyantābhyāṃ vākyābhyāṃ pūrvavadupajīvyate /
tena madhyadīpakatā /
children.translated_text: <s>Yātapatikās</s> are women whose husbands have gone abroad. Because autumn is contextually relevant, and because dwelling in foreign lands and the sight of women whose husbands have departed are contextually irrelevant, here there is implicit comparison. And here, the property characterized by being the sole cause of the suffering of travelers — [namely] 'the sight of women whose husbands have departed was only for suffering' — taken up in the middle sentence, is drawn upon by the first and last sentences as before. Therefore it is <s>madhya-dīpaka</s> (illumination in the middle).
Example of <s>anta-dīpaka</s> (illumination at the end):
At that time, overflowing with the radiance of abundant beauty,
the face of the beloved and the moon — for whom was either not a source of delight?

children.text:
tadānīṃ śaratsamaye /
atra induḥ prākaraṇikaḥ śaratsamayasya upavarṇyamānatvāt /

children.translated_text: The face of the beloved (<s>kāntānana-indu</s>, 'moon of the beloved's face') is contextually irrelevant.

children.text: ante ca sarvasukhahetutvamupanibaddhaṃ sat pūrvatra upajīvyate /
children.translated_text: And the property of being the cause of all happiness, incorporated at the end, is drawn upon by what precedes.
Therefore here it is <s>anta-dīpaka</s> (illumination at the end).
Thus this <s>dīpaka</s> has been defined and illustrated.
At that time: during the autumn season. Here the moon (<s>indu</s>) is contextually relevant, because the autumn season is being described.

children.text:
nanu upamāyā 'upamā dīpakaṃ ca'iti pūrvamaddiṣṭatvāt yathoddeśalakṣaṇamiti nyāyāttsyā eva pūrvaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ kartavyam, paścāttu dīpakasya /
tatkathamādau dīpakaṃ lakṣitamiti vaktavyam /
ucyate /
anena graṃthakṛtā svoparacitakumārasaṃbhavaikadeśo 'tra udāharaṇatvenopanyastaḥ /
takṣa pūrvaṃ dīpakasyodāharaṇāni /

children.translated_text: Here, the order of enumeration was abandoned
for the sake of not breaking the continuity of that textual connection.
But the enumeration was not made in that way, out of fear of breaking the meter.
Similarly, in subsequent definitions too, the justification for not following the order of enumeration should be stated.

Now, since <s>upamā</s> (simile) was enumerated earlier in '<s>upamā</s> and <s>dīpaka</s>,' by the principle that 'definition should follow the order of enumeration,' the definition of <s>upamā</s> should have been given first, and that of <s>dīpaka</s> afterwards. So how was <s>dīpaka</s> defined first? — this must be explained. The answer is: The author of the treatise has presented here, as an illustration, a passage from his own composition, the <s>Kumārasaṃbhava</s>. In that, the illustrations of <s>dīpaka</s> come first.
<s>Upamā</s> (simile):
That which is a captivating similarity between the <s>upamāna</s> (standard of comparison) and the <s>upameya</s> (object of comparison),
of two words whose grounds of application — such as time and the like — are mutually distinct, that is <s>upamā</s> (simile). [UKss 1.15]
Through the use of words like <s>yathā</s> (as) and <s>iva</s> (like), it is entitled to denotative connection (<s>śruti</s>).
Otherwise, through the attachment of words like <s>sadṛśa</s> (similar) and the like, it is said to be twofold. [UKss 1.16]
Even when expressed concisely, this [simile] is bound
by the separation of the similarity-expressing word, the <s>upameya</s> (object of comparison), and its designator. [UKss 1.17]
In the statement of <s>upamāna</s> (standard) and <s>upameya</s> (object), through the separation of the similarity [word] and its designator,
sometimes in a compound, without the designator, and sometimes with it — [UKss 1.18]
likewise, from the <s>upamāna</s> (standard), through a statement powered by the <s>kyac</s> suffix denoting behavior,

children.text: kvacitsā karturācāre kyaṅā sā ca kvipā kvacit // UKss_1.19 //
children.translated_text: sometimes it [arises] from the behavior of the agent through <s>kyaṅ</s>, and sometimes through the zero-suffix (<s>kvip</s>). [UKss 1.19]

children.text: upamāne karmaṇi vā kartari vā yo ṇamulkaṣādagataḥ /
children.translated_text: When the <s>ṇamul</s> suffix, drawn from the <s>upamāna</s>, [applies] to the object or to the agent,

children.text: tadvācyā sā vatinā ca karma sāmānyavacanena // UKss_1.20 //
children.translated_text: it is expressed by that; and also by the <s>vati</s> suffix and by a general term for action. [UKss 1.20]
And by the <s>vati</s> suffix derived from a noun ending in the sixth or seventh case, to express that [comparison];

children.text: kalpatprabhṛtibhiranyaiśca taddhitaiḥ sā nibadhyate kavibhiḥ // UKss_1.21 //
children.translated_text: and by other secondary suffixes (<s>taddhitas</s>) such as <s>kalpa</s> and so forth, it is bound by poets. [UKss 1.21]

children.text:
sādṛśyasaṃbandhitvenopādīyate yatprākaraṇikaṃ tadupameyam /
na khalu prākaraṇikasyāpi sādṛśyasaṃbandhitvena anupādīyamānasyopameyatā, yathā rājñaḥ puruṣamānayetyatra puruṣasya /
puruṣo hyatrānīyamānatvena codyamānatvātsatyapi prākaraṇikatve sādṛsyasaṃbandhitvenānupādīyamānatvānnopameyaḥ /
satyapi ca sādṛśyasaṃbandhitvenopādāne yasya prākaraṇikatvaṃ nāsti tasyopamānatvaṃ, na tūpameyatvamiti prākaraṇikamityuktam /
tadevaṃ sādṛśyasaṃbandhitvenopādīyamānaṃ yatprākaraṇikaṃ tadupameyam /
taddhyupamānena sādṛśyapratipādanadvāreṇa samīpe kṣipyate tasmādupameyam /
aprākaraṇikaṃ tu tathāvidhamevopamānam /
tayorupamānopameyayoryatsādharmyaṃ samāno dharmaḥ tena dharmeṇa saṃbandho yaḥ sā upamānopameyayoḥ sādṛśyadvāreṇa sābhīpyaparicchedahetutvādupamā /
tasyāścālaṅkārādhikārāccetohāritvaṃ labdhameva /
kāvyaśobhāvahānāṃ dharmāṇāṃ guṇavyatiriktatve satyalaṅkāratvāt /
guṇāḥ khalu kāvyaśobhāhetavo dharmāḥ /
te ca mādhuryaujaḥprasādalakṣaṇāḥ yeṣāṃ tu guṇopajanitaśobhe kāvye śobhātiśayahetutvaṃ te 'laṅkārāḥ /
yadavocadbhaṭṭavāmanaḥ----
'kāvyaśobhāyāḥ kartāro dharmā guṇāḥ /
tadatiśayahetavastvalaṅkārāḥ"iti tenālaṅakāratvādevopamāyāścetohāritvaṃ labdham /
ataścetohārītyanuvādaḥ /
prāptārthatvāt /
upamānopameyabhāvaśca nātyantaṃ sādharmyeṇa upādāne sati bhavati gaurivāyaṃ gauriti /
ata uktaṃ mithovibhinnakālādiśabdayoriti /
kālādayo 'tra śabdapravṛttinimittabhūtā vivakṣitāḥ /
keṣāṃcitkhalu śabdānāṃ svārthe pravartamānānāṃ kālaḥ pravṛttinimittam, yathā vasantādīnāma /
keṣāṃcitta dik, yathā prācyādīnām /
keṣāṃcijjātiryathā gavādīnām /
śuklaprabhṛtīnāṃ tu guṇaḥ /
gacchatyādīnāṃ kriyā /
rājapuruṣādīnāṃ svasvāmibhāvādiḥ saṃbandhaḥ /
evamanyadapyanusartavyam /
mithaḥ parasparaṃ vibhinnāḥ kālādayaḥ pravṛttinimittabhūtā yayoḥ śabdayostathāvidhau śabdau vācakau yayorupamānopameyayoriti bahuvrīhigarbho bahuvrīhiḥ /
gaurivāyaṃ gaurityabhidhāne tu na pravṛttinimittabhedaḥ /
gotvasyaivaikasya pravṛttinimittatvāt /
tena evaṃvidha upamānopameyabhāvo na bhavati /
'upamā tu tat'ityatra vākye tuśabdo 'laṅkārāntare vyatireke /
upamā punarevaṃprakāretyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: That which is contextually relevant and is adopted by virtue of being related to similarity — that is the <s>upameya</s> (object of comparison). Indeed, even something contextually relevant, if it is not adopted as related to similarity, is not an <s>upameya</s>, as for instance the 'person' in 'Bring the king's person.' For the person here, even though contextually relevant, is not the <s>upameya</s> because it is brought up in the capacity of being led, not as related to similarity. And even when something is adopted as related to similarity, if it is not contextually relevant, it has the status of <s>upamāna</s> (standard of comparison), not of <s>upameya</s> — hence the word 'contextually relevant' was used. Thus, that which is contextually relevant and adopted as related to similarity — that is the <s>upameya</s>. For it is cast near [the <s>upamāna</s>] through the medium of establishing similarity with the <s>upamāna</s>; hence [it is called] <s>upameya</s>. And that which is of the same kind but not contextually relevant is the <s>upamāna</s>. Of those two — the <s>upamāna</s> and the <s>upameya</s> — the common property (<s>sādharmya</s>), i.e., the shared attribute, and the connection with that attribute — that, by being the cause of determining proximity through similarity between the <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s>, is <s>upamā</s> (simile). And its quality of being captivating (<s>cetohāritva</s>) is already obtained by virtue of its being in the domain of <s>alaṅkāra</s> (poetic figure). For the properties that bring beauty to poetry, when they are other than <s>guṇas</s> (excellences), are <s>alaṅkāras</s>. <s>Guṇas</s> indeed are the properties that cause the beauty of poetry. And they are characterized as <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness), <s>ojas</s> (vigor), and <s>prasāda</s> (lucidity). Those that cause a surpassing of beauty in poetry whose beauty is produced by <s>guṇas</s> — those are <s>alaṅkāras</s>. As <s>Bhaṭṭa Vāmana</s> said: '<s>Guṇas</s> are the properties that create the beauty of poetry. <s>Alaṅkāras</s> are the causes of surpassing that.'
