And this mutual relation of <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s> here is grounded in the absence of any other standard of comparison.

children.text: yadi parametayoreva parasparamupamānopameyabhāvaḥ syādanyatve tayorupamānaṃ nāstīti //
children.translated_text: If indeed the mutual relation of <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s> obtains between these two alone, it is because there is no other standard of comparison for them.

Here, by taking up the word 'yasya' (whose) and connecting it with the pronoun 'tat' in the verse 'tvatkṛte so 'pi <s>Vaikuṇṭha</s>,' the syntactic expectation will be resolved.
And in the subsequent verses too, the meaning of the relative pronoun 'yat' should be made syntactically complete by that same [correlative].
<s>Sahokti</s> (simultaneous statement):
Where two actions pertaining to two different things occurring at the same time

children.text: padenaikena kathyete sā sahoktirmatā satām // UKss_5.15 //
children.translated_text: are expressed by a single word — that is considered <s>sahokti</s> by the learned. (UKss 5.15)

children.text:
yatra vastudvayasamavete dve kriye padenaikena tantravṛttyā kathyete tatra sahoktirnāmālaṅkāro bhavati /
nanu 'saṃjahāra śaratkālaḥ'ityādāvapi dīpake padenaikena vastudvayasamavete dve kriye kathyete /
ataśca tatrāpi sahoktitvaṃ prāpnotīti āsaṅkyoktam---tulyakāle iti /
yatra sahādinā padena tulyakālatāmavagamya vastudvitayasamāśrite dve kriye kathyete tatra sahoktitvam /
na caivaṃ dīpaka iti nātivyāptiḥ /
sahādinā ca śabdena yugapatkālatāyāmavadyotyamānāyāṃ dvaya gatiḥ /
kadācitkhalu yayoḥ kriyayostulyakālatā te kriye tulyakakṣatayā svāśrayaviśrāntatvenābhidhīyete, yatā devadattyajñadattau saha bhuñjāte iti kadācittvekāśrayaviśrāntāyāṃ kriyāyāmabhihitāyāṃ sahādyarthaparyālocanāsāmarthyādaparasyāśrayasya kriyāsaṃbandho 'vagamyate, yathā devadatto yajñadattena saha bhūṅkta iti /
tatreha dvitīyā gatirāśrīyate /
śābdena rūpeṇaikatra kriyāsaṃbandhasya pratītasyāparatrārthena rūpeṇonnīyamānatvena vakrabhaṇite sadbhāvāt /
evaṃvidhasya yatraiva śobhātiśayavidhāyitvaṃ tatraiva sahokteralaṅkāratā na sarvatreti draṣṭavyam /
tasyā udāharaṇam----
children.translated_text:
Where two actions pertaining to two different things are expressed by a single word through the device of <s>tantravṛtti</s> (single operation serving dual purpose), there the figure called <s>sahokti</s> obtains.
Now, in cases like '<s>Śarat</s> season withdrew' and so on, in <s>dīpaka</s> (illuminator) too, two actions pertaining to two things are expressed by a single word.
Therefore, since <s>sahokti</s> would apply there too, anticipating this objection it is stated: 'at the same time.'
Where, by ascertaining simultaneity through a word such as 'saha' (together), two actions pertaining to two things are expressed, there <s>sahokti</s> applies.
But this is not so in <s>dīpaka</s>, hence there is no over-extension.
And through the word 'saha' and the like, when simultaneity of time is indicated, there are two possible constructions:
Sometimes the two actions that are simultaneous are expressed as being of equal status, each resting in its own subject, as in '<s>Devadatta</s> and <s>Yajñadatta</s> eat together.' Sometimes, when one action resting in one subject is expressed, through the interpretive force of the meaning of 'saha' and the like, the relation of action to the other subject is understood, as in '<s>Devadatta</s> eats together with <s>Yajñadatta</s>.'
Here the second construction is adopted.
Because the oblique expression obtains when the relation of action, understood verbally with respect to one subject, is inferred by implication with respect to the other.
Only where such a construction produces an abundance of beauty does <s>sahokti</s> have the status of a figure of speech, not everywhere — this should be understood.
An example of it:
The celestial host, together with <s>Mṛtyu</s> (Death), in his battle called <s>Tārakāmaya</s>,
accomplished their desired ends through the one called <s>Cakra</s> (discus), who was his servant. (UKss 5.*15)

children.text:
yasya praiṣyeṇa iti saṃbandhaḥ /
atra mṛtyordyujanasya ca manorathāvāptikaraṇalakṣaṇe dve kriye padenaikenokte cakre 'vāptamanoratha iti /
yadyapyavāptamanoratha iti cakra iti ca suptiḍantatvabhedena padadvitvaṃ tathāpi kriyāpadadvitayopādānavyāvṛttervavakṣitatvātpadenaikeneti na virudhyate /
athavā cakre iti karoti kriyā sāmānyabhūtā viśeṣamantareṇāparyavasyantī manorathāvāptilakṣaṇaṃ viśeṣaṃ garbhīkaroti /
ataścātra satyapyanekapadatve ekapadībhāva iva prakāśate /

children.translated_text: Hence it is said 'by a single word.'
And the word 'sārdham' (together) here indicates the simultaneity of time.

children.text: yasya praiṣyeṇājñākāriṇā cakrasaṃjñakena kartṛbhūtena mṛtyunā sārdhamapṛthakkālatayā dyujana āptamanorathaḥ kṛta iti /
children.translated_text: By whose servant — one who carries out commands — named <s>Cakra</s>, acting as the agent, together with <s>Mṛtyu</s> (Death), simultaneously, the celestial host had their desires fulfilled — this is the meaning.
The fulfillment of <s>Mṛtyu</s>'s desire is due to the devouring of many worlds, and of the celestial host due to the destruction of enemies.

The syntactic connection is: 'yasya praiṣyeṇa' (by whose servant).
Here, the two actions characterized as the fulfillment of desires of <s>Mṛtyu</s> and the celestial host are expressed by a single word — 'cakre' (accomplished) and 'āptamanoratha' (one whose desire is fulfilled).
Although there is duality of words due to the distinction between nominal and verbal endings in 'āptamanoratha' and 'cakre,' nevertheless, since the intended meaning excludes the employment of two action-words, the statement 'by a single word' is not contradicted.
Alternatively, 'cakre' (did/made) is a general action that, without culminating in a specific meaning, incorporates the specific meaning of the fulfillment of desires.
Therefore, even though there are multiple words here, it appears as if there were a single word.
<s>Parivṛtti</s> (exchange):
The exchange of something with that which is equal, inferior, or superior,
which is of the nature of gain or loss — that is declared to be <s>parivṛtti</s>. (UKss 5.16)

children.text:
kasyacidvastuno vastvantareṇa parivartanaṃ parivṛttiḥ /
sā ca trividhā /
parivartanakārakāṇāṃ parivartanīyena saha samatvānnyūnatvādadhikatvācca /
tadidamuktam--samanyūnaviśiṣṭairiti /
tatra yasyāḥ samor'thaḥ parivartyate tasyā anarthasvabhāvatā /
arthaśabdena hi upādeyo 'ptho 'bhidhīyater,'thyate 'sāviti kṛtvā /
yatra ca sāmyaṃ tabhārthanīyatvaṃ nāsti /
tenārthyatvābhāvānugamāttatrānarthatvamabhidhīyate /
atastatrānarthasvabhāvaṃ parivartanam /
yatrāpa ca nikṛṣṭaparigraheṇotkṛṣṭaparityāgaḥ kriyate, tatrāpyanarthasvabhāvatā /
upādeyaviparītasyopādānāt /
arthapratipakṣo hyatrānarthaḥ /
adharmānṛtavat /
yatā hyadharmānṛtaśabdābhyāṃ nottarapadārthrābhāvamātramabhidhīyate, nāpyuttarapadārthatulyor'thaḥ, kiṃ tarhi etatpratipakṣasyaivābhidhānaṃ, evamihāpyanarthaśabdena arthapratipakṣasyaivābhidhanam /
yathā anartho vairiṇāmāpatita ityevamādau /
tena yatrotkṛṣṭena nikṛṣṭaḥ parigṛhyate tatra duḥkhahetutvādarahthapratipakṣatvenānarthakhabhāvatā /
yatra tu nikṛṣṭenotkṛṣṭaḥ parigṛhyate tatrotkṛṣṭasya sukhahetutvenopādeyatvādarthasvabhāvatā /
tadidamuktam---arthānarthasvabhāvamiti /
tatra samaparivṛtterudāharaṇam---
children.translated_text:
The exchange of one thing with another thing is <s>parivṛtti</s>.
It is of three kinds.
Due to the equality, inferiority, or superiority of the exchanging agents with respect to what is being exchanged.
This is stated as 'with those that are equal, inferior, or superior.'
Therein, that [exchange] in which what is equal is exchanged is of the nature of loss.
For by the word 'artha' (gain/value) what is desirable is denoted, since it is 'sought after' (arthyate).
And where there is equality, there is no desirability.
Therefore, from the concomitance of the absence of desirability, loss is predicated of it.
Hence the exchange there is of the nature of loss.
And where the abandonment of something superior is made in favor of accepting something inferior, there too it is of the nature of loss.
Because what is the opposite of the desirable is accepted.
For 'anartha' (loss) here means the opposite of 'artha' (gain),
like 'adharma' (unrighteousness) and 'anṛta' (untruth).
Just as by the words 'adharma' and 'anṛta,' not merely the absence of the meaning of the latter member is denoted, nor a meaning equal to the latter member, but rather the very opposite of it is denoted — likewise here too, by the word 'anartha,' the very opposite of gain is denoted,
as in 'misfortune has befallen the enemies' and so on.
Therefore, where something inferior is accepted in place of something superior, there, being the cause of suffering, it is of the nature of loss as the opposite of gain.
But where something superior is accepted in place of something inferior, there, since the superior is desirable as the cause of happiness, it is of the nature of gain.
This is stated as 'of the nature of gain or loss.'
An example of exchange with an equal:
He who, having given his chest to the enemies of the gods in battles, obtained
glory together with the goddess of victory, in the slaying of <s>Hiraṇyākṣa</s> and others. (UKss 5.*16)

children.text:
atra urodānena utsāho lakṣyate yaścātra lakṣyamāṇāsyārthasyotsāhasyopāyatayā pratīyate /
abhidheyor'tho vakṣaso dānaṃ nāma yo hi yatra vakṣa udyamayati sa tatrotsahata iti tatpratibhāvacchāditasyotasāhasya pratitiḥ tadapekṣayā samena samasya parivartanam /
uroyaśasoḥ samatvāt /
children.translated_text:
Here, by the giving of the chest, valor is indicated, and the valor thus indicated is understood as the means to the end that is the intended meaning.
The denoted meaning is the giving of the chest — for he who exerts his chest in a place, he makes an effort there — thus valor, concealed by the figurative meaning, is understood. In relation to that, the exchange is of an equal with an equal,
due to the equality of the chest and glory.
An example of exchange with an inferior:
With the jewels that fell from the summit of Mount <s>Mandara</s>, whirling as the serpent serving as the rope trembled,

children.text: ratnairāpūrya dugdhārbdhi yaḥ samādatta kaustubham // UKss_5.*17 //
children.translated_text: having filled the ocean of milk, he took the <s>Kaustubha</s> gem. (UKss 5.*17)

children.text:
netrabhūta urago vāsukiḥ /
atra--kaustubhasyotkṛṣṭasya nikṛṣṭaratnaparatyāgena grahaṇānnikṛṣṭenotkṛṣṭasya parivartanam /
children.translated_text:
The serpent serving as the rope is <s>Vāsuki</s>.
Here — the acceptance of the superior <s>Kaustubha</s> through the relinquishment of inferior jewels is the exchange of something superior by means of something inferior.
An example of exchange with a superior:

children.text: yo balau vyāptabhūsīmna makhena dyāṃ jigīṣati /
children.translated_text: He who, when <s>Bali</s> had conquered the boundaries of the earth, sought to win heaven through a sacrifice;

children.text: abhayaṃ svargasadmabhyo datvā jagrāha kharvatam // UKss_5.*18 //
children.translated_text: having given fearlessness to the dwellers of heaven, he assumed a dwarfish form. (UKss 5.*18)

children.text:
bhūsīmā pṛthivyā avadhiḥ /
makho yajñaḥ /
atra abhayenotkṛṣṭena nikṛṣṭasya kharvatvasya hrasvatvasya parivartanaṃ abhidheyāpekṣayā
children.translated_text:
'Bhūsīmā' means the boundary of the earth.
'Makha' means sacrifice.
Here, the exchange of the inferior dwarfish form by means of the superior fearlessness, from the perspective of the denoted meaning,

children.text:
pūrvatarodāharaṇavatpratibhāti /
tātparyārthāpekṣayā tu neyaṃ parivṛttiḥ /
cattaddevebhyaḥ abhayaṃ pratijñātaṃ tadupāyabhūtāyā vāmanaveṣeṇa svarvatāyāḥ parigṛhītatvāt /
children.translated_text:
appears like the earlier example.
But from the perspective of the intended purport, this is not [a disadvantageous] <s>parivṛtti</s>,
since the fearlessness promised to the gods was accepted as the means, through the assumption of the <s>Vāmana</s> (dwarf) form.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the concise commentary on <s>Udbhaṭa</s>'s <s>Alaṅkārasārasaṃgraha</s>, composed by the illustrious <s>Pratīhāra Indurāja</s>.
Now the sixth chapter.
<s>Ananvaya</s> (non-correlation), <s>sasaṃdeha</s> (doubt), <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (combination), <s>bhāvika</s> (the evocative),
<s>kāvyadṛṣṭānta</s> (poetic example), and <s>hetu</s> (reason) — these figures of speech the learned know. (UKss 6.1)

children.text:
atra itiśabdasya vakṣyamāṇaṃ yadananvayādilakṣaṇaṃ tadupakṣepārthatvena prayogānnānanvayādisvarūpaparāmarśārthatvam /
ityevaṃ vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇakatvenānanvayādīnalaṅkārānvidurityarthaḥ /
ityevaṃ vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇakatvenānanvayādīnalaṅkārānvidurityarthaḥ /
ato vedanakriyākarmatvādananvayamityādau dvitīyā /
kāvyadṛṣṭāntahetū cetyatra dṛṣṭāntahetuśabdābhyāṃ kāvyaśabdaḥ pratyekamabhisaṃbadhyate /
dṛṣṭāntaśabdasya cātra pūrvanipāto 'bhyarhitatvāt /
abhyarhitatvaṃ dṛṣṭāntasya dṛṣṭāntapratibimbitavyāptimukhena hetoḥ prāyeṇa gamakatā saṃpratyayāt /
children.translated_text:
Here, the word 'iti' is used to introduce the forthcoming definitions of <s>ananvaya</s> and the rest, not to refer back to their nature.
The meaning is: the learned know <s>ananvaya</s> and the other figures as having the definitions that will be stated hereafter.
Therefore, because <s>ananvaya</s> and the rest are objects of the verb 'know' (vidanti), the accusative case is used in 'ananvayam' and so on.
In '<s>kāvyadṛṣṭānta</s> and <s>hetu</s>,' the word '<s>kāvya</s>' is connected individually with both '<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>' and '<s>hetu</s>.'
The word '<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>' is placed first here because of its greater eminence.
The eminence of <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> is recognized from the fact that <s>hetu</s> (reason) generally leads to understanding through the medium of the <s>vyāpti</s> (universal concomitance) that is reflected in the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example).
<s>Sasaṃdeha</s> (doubt):

children.text: upamānena tattvaṃ ca bhedaṃ ca vadataḥ punaḥ /
children.translated_text: When one states both the identity and the difference with the standard of comparison,

children.text: sasaṃdehaṃ vacaḥ stutyai sasaṃdehaṃ vadurbudhāḥ // UKss_6.2 //
children.translated_text: a statement involving doubt, for the sake of praise — the wise call that <s>sasaṃdeha</s>. (UKss 6.2)

children.text:
upamānabhedapūrvaṃ bhedamabhidadhataḥ kaveḥ kavinibaddhasya vā vakturvaca iti saṃbandhaḥ /
saṃdehopetavacanavyājena upamānena tattvaṃ tadbhāvamabhedamupameyasyābhidhāyottarakālaṃ yadā tasmādupamānāttasyopameyasya bhedo 'bhidhīyate tadā sasaṃdeho 'laṅkāraḥ /
nanu upamānena saha pūrvamabhede 'bhihite sati punaryadi tasmāddhedasyābhidhānaṃ kriyate /
evaṃ sati gajasnānaṃ prāpnotītyāśaṅkyoktam----stutyai iti /
stutyarthatvena evaṃvidhā abhidhā samāśrīyata ityarthaḥ /
tasyodāharaṇam----
children.translated_text:
The syntactic connection is: the speech of a poet who states difference after [stating] identity with the <s>upamāna</s>, or of a speaker portrayed in poetry.
When, by the device of a statement involving doubt, having first stated the identity — the non-difference — of the <s>upameya</s> with the <s>upamāna</s>, subsequently the difference of that <s>upameya</s> from that <s>upamāna</s> is stated, then the figure <s>sasaṃdeha</s> obtains.
Now, if after first stating non-difference with the <s>upamāna</s>, the statement of difference from it is then made,
then it would result in futility like bathing an elephant — anticipating this objection it is stated: 'for the sake of praise.'
The meaning is: such a mode of expression is adopted for the purpose of praise.
An example of it:
Is this in his hand a mass of glory born from the complete destruction of enemies' hearts?
If it were a mass of glory, what would cause its spherical form? (UKss 6.*1)
Is this a swan that has come longing for the lotus of his navel? No, this is not fickle.
Thus, the guileless people around him wondered about the conch. (UKss 6.*2)

children.text:
ārjavo mūrkhaḥ /
ṛjutvayogāt /
atra śaṅkha upameyaḥ /
yaśaḥsaṃcayo haṃsaścopamānam /
tayośca pūrvamabhedasaṃdehavyājenābhihitaḥ kimeṣa yaśaḥsaṃcayaḥ syāditi, tathā kiṃ haṃsa iti punaścātropamānādupameyasya bhedo varṇitaḥ /
yaśaḥsaṃcayāttāvadbhedopavarṇanaṃ piṇḍībhāvo 'sya kiṃkṛta ita /
yaśaḥsaṃcayaḥ khalu prasaraṇaśīlaḥ /
asya tu tadviruddhaḥ piṇḍībhāvo dṛśyate /
tena nāyaṃ yaśaḥsaṃcaya iti /

children.translated_text: And the statement of difference from the swan is: 'this is not fickle.'
For fickleness is a characteristic property of the swan.
And here that is not perceived; therefore this is certainly not a swan.

children.text: evaṃ vidhasya cātrābhidhānasya phalaṃ stutiḥ, yaśaḥsaṃcayo bhagavatā svahastavartī kṛta iti, tathāsaṃbhāvyamānahaṃsāgamanaṃ tribhuvanotpattinibandhanaṃ yattannābhinalinaṃ tadvān bhagavāniti //
children.translated_text: And the purpose of such a statement here is praise: that the mass of glory has been made to rest in the hand of the Lord; and likewise, the Lord possesses that lotus of the navel which is the cause of the creation of the three worlds, to which even the swan, whose coming is inconceivable, has arrived.

'Ārjava' means a simpleton,
due to possessing straightforwardness.
Here the conch is the <s>upameya</s>.
The mass of glory and the swan are the <s>upamāna</s>.
And of these, first non-difference is stated by the device of doubt — 'Is this a mass of glory?' and likewise 'Is this a swan?' — and then the difference of the <s>upameya</s> from the <s>upamāna</s> is described.
The description of difference from the mass of glory is: 'what would cause its spherical form?'
For a mass of glory is by nature diffusive.
But its opposite, a spherical form, is seen in this.
Therefore this is not a mass of glory.
He states another variety of <s>sasaṃdeha</s>:
That which, having produced the semblance of another figure, creates a binding effect in the minds [of listeners],
and which takes the form of doubt even where there is no [real] doubt — that is called <s>saṃdeha</s>. (UKss 6.3)

children.text:
chāyā śobhā /
yatra saṃdehābhāve 'pi saṃdehasyopanibandhe sati na pūrvavadupamānādupameyasya bheda upanibadhyate kiṃtarhyabheda eva saṃśayacchāyayā /
tathāvidhasya copanibandhasya phalamalaṅkārāntaropajanitā saundaryapratipattiḥ /
yadāha---dhīṣvalaṅkārāntaracchāyāṃ kṛtvā iti /
tatrāpi saṃdehālaṅkāraḥ /
children.translated_text:
'Chāyā' means beauty or semblance.
Where, even in the absence of doubt, when doubt is superimposed, the difference of the <s>upameya</s> from the <s>upamāna</s> is not stated as before, but rather non-difference alone [is presented] with the appearance of doubt —
and the purpose of such a superimposition is the apprehension of beauty produced by another figure.
As stated: 'having produced the semblance of another figure in the minds.'
There too the figure is <s>saṃdeha</s>.
An example of it:
Is this a dark cloud on <s>Meru</s>, or smoke in the fire of cosmic dissolution?

children.text: iti yaḥ śaṅkyate śyāmaḥ pakṣīndrerkatviṣi sthitaḥ // UKss_6.*3 //
children.translated_text: Thus the dark one, seated on the radiance of <s>Garuḍa</s>, the lord of birds, is wondered about. (UKss 6.*3)

children.text:
atra meroruparivartī nīlo balāhakaḥ kalpāntavahnyāścayaśca dhūmaḥ ityetadubhayamupamānam /
garuḍārūḍhastu bhagavān kṛṣṇavapurupameyaḥ /
tena ca upamānadvayena saṃdehavyājena bhagavānāpāditābheda upanibaddhaḥ kimayamevaṃvidhaḥ athaivaṃvidhaḥ iti /
tābhyāṃ copamānābhyāmupameyasya pūrvavadbhedanibandhanaṃ nātra kiṃcidabhihitam /
phalaṃ caivamabhidhānasyopamālaṅkāradhvananam /
evaṃvidhopamānadvitayasadṛśo bhagavānvainateyārūḍha iti /
children.translated_text:
Here, a dark rain-cloud hovering over <s>Meru</s> and the smoke of the fire at the end of the aeon — both of these are the <s>upamāna</s>.
But the Lord, of dark complexion, mounted on <s>Garuḍa</s>, is the <s>upameya</s>.
With those two standards of comparison, the Lord is presented as non-different through the device of doubt — 'is this such-and-such, or is this such-and-such?'
And with those two <s>upamāna</s>s, no statement of the difference of the <s>upameya</s> is made here as before.
And the purpose of such a statement is the suggestion of the figure of <s>upamā</s> (simile).
The Lord mounted on <s>Vainateya</s> (<s>Garuḍa</s>) resembles both such standards of comparison.
<s>Ananvaya</s> (non-correlation):
Where a thing's own standard-and-object-of-comparison relation exists by that very [thing] itself —
because of the intention to express incomparability — that, they say, is <s>ananvaya</s> (self-comparison).

children.text:
yatra tenaiva na tu vastvantareṇa tasyaiva vastvantarasyopamānopameyabhāvo bhavettatra vastvantarānugamābhāvādananvayākhyo 'laṅkāraḥ /
nanu ca sādṛśyasaṃbandhe sati prākaraṇikamupameyamaprākaraṇikaṃ tūpamānamityupamānopameyayorlakṣitatvātkathamekasyaivopamitikriyāyāṃ karmatvaṃ karaṇatvaṃ ca saṃbhavatītyāśaṅkyoktam---asādṛśyavivakṣāta iti /
nātromapānopameyabhāve tātparyaṃ kintūpameyopamāvadupamānāntaravyāvṛttāvityarthaḥ /
itiśabde 'tra vakṣyamāṇodāharaṇopakṣepārthatvādananvayaśabdena nābhisaṃbadhyate /
tena ananvayamiti dvitīyā /
children.translated_text: Where the relation of standard of comparison (<s>upamāna</s>) and object of comparison (<s>upameya</s>) of a thing exists with that very thing itself, and not with another thing — there, because of the absence of following upon another thing, the figure called <s>ananvaya</s> (self-comparison) [arises]. Now, [objection:] since the <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s> are defined such that, when a relation of similarity obtains, the contextually relevant is the <s>upameya</s> and the contextually irrelevant is the <s>upamāna</s> — how can one and the same thing have both the status of object (<s>karmatva</s>) and instrument (<s>karaṇatva</s>) in the action of comparison? Anticipating this, it was said: 'because of the intention to express incomparability.' The purport here is not the relation of <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s>, but rather the exclusion of any other standard of comparison, as in simile where the object of comparison [stands alone]. The word '<s>iti</s>' here does not connect with the word '<s>ananvaya</s>' because it serves to introduce the forthcoming example. Therefore '<s>ananvayam</s>' is in the accusative case.
Its example:
He whose speech is like his own speech, whose spotless action is like his own action,

children.text: rūpaṃ svamiva rūpaṃ ca lokalocanalobhanam // UKss_6.*4 //
children.translated_text: whose form is like his own form — captivating the eyes of the world.

children.text: atra vāṇīkriyārūpāṇāṃ trayāṇāmanupamatayā lokottaratvaṃ pratipādayitumātmanaivopamānopameyabhāvo nibaddhaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, to convey the transcendent nature of his speech, action, and form — these three — through their incomparability, the relation of standard and object of comparison is composed with himself alone.
<s>Saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (combination of figures):
The co-occurrence in one [passage] of many ornaments (<s>alaṅkṛti</s>), or of two,
that are mutually independent — that is called <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (combination).

children.text:
bahūnāmalaṅkārāṇāṃ parasparanirapekṣāṇāṃ dvayorvā tathāvidhayorekatra śabda eva artha eva vā upanibandhe sati saṃsṛṣṭiralaṅkāraḥ /
yatra tu parasparasāpekṣatvaṃ tatra sandehaikaśabdābhidhānānugrāhyānugrāhakasaṅkarāstrayaḥ pūrvamabhihitāḥ /
yatra ca śabdārthalakṣaṇāśrayadvitayaniṣṭhatayā anekālaṅkāropanibandhastatrāpi śabdārthavartyanekālaṅkārasaṃkara uktaḥ /
etadvailakṣaṇyena tu saṃsṛṣṭiḥ /
tasyā udāharaṇam-----
children.translated_text: When many ornaments that are mutually independent, or two such, are bound together in one [passage] — in the words alone or in the meaning alone — that is the figure <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s>. But where there is mutual dependence, there the three types of <s>saṅkara</s> (conflation) — namely <s>sandeha</s> (doubt), <s>ekaśabdābhidhāna</s> (single-word designation), and <s>anugrāhyānugrāhaka</s> (supporter-supported) — were previously stated. And where, by virtue of culminating in both bases — namely word and meaning — there is the binding together of multiple ornaments, there too the conflation of multiple ornaments occurring in word and meaning has been stated. It is by contrast with that [conflation] that <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> [is defined]. Its example:
For your sake, even that <s>Vaikuṇṭha</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>), like the moon at dawn [abandoning] moonlight,

children.text: apyadhārāṃ sudhāvṛrṣṭi manye tyajati tāṃ śriyam // UKss_6.*5 //
children.translated_text: even abandons — a ceaseless shower of nectar, I think — that <s>Śrī</s> (Lakṣmī).
Therefore arise, O lotus-eyed one, with some exceedingly fortunate

children.text: vareṇa saha tāruṇyaṃ nirviśantī gṛhe vasa // UKss_6.*6 //
children.translated_text: husband, enjoying your youth — dwell in [his] house.

children.text:
nirviśantī upabhuñjānā /
atra śaśī uṣasi candrikāmiva vaikuṇṭhaḥ tvatkṛte śriyaṃ tyajati ityupamā /
adhārāṃ sudhāvṛṣṭimiti rūpakam /

tathā hyatra lakṣmyāḥ sarve pīyūṣavṛṣṭeḥ saṃbandhino dharmā vidyante kevalaṃ dhārāsaṃbandho nāstītyupamānagataikaguṇanivṛttidvārikā śiṣṭopamānagatasakalaguṇābhyanujñārūpāropaṇāvagamyate, yathā ayaṃ puruṣaḥ akaro hastīti /
children.translated_text: For thus, here <s>Lakṣmī</s> possesses all the properties related to a shower of nectar, except only the connection with a stream — and through the door of the cessation of one quality belonging to the standard of comparison, the superimposition in the form of granting all remaining qualities of the standard is understood, just as [in] 'this man is an elephant without a trunk.'

children.text: tadetasmin śloke upamāyā rūpakasya ca dvayoralaṅkārayoḥ saṃsṛṣṭiḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus in this verse there is <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> (combination) of the two ornaments, <s>upamā</s> (simile) and <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor).
Because both of them reside solely in the expressed meaning, and because they are mutually independent.

children.text: 'taduttiṣṭha'ityetacchlokāpekṣayā tu 'kamalekṣaṇe'iti samāsopamātmakamupamābhedamāśritya pūrvoktālaṅkāradvayasaṃkalanayā bahūnā malaṅkārāṇāṃ saṃsṛṣṭyudāharaṇadikpradarśanaṃ draṣṭavyam //
children.translated_text: With reference to the verse 'therefore arise,' by resort to the variety of <s>upamā</s> consisting of a compound-simile (<s>samāsopamā</s>) in '<s>kamalekṣaṇe</s>' (lotus-eyed one), combined with the two previously mentioned ornaments, this should be seen as an indication of the direction of an example of the <s>saṃsṛṣṭi</s> of many ornaments.

'<s>Nirviśantī</s>' means enjoying. Here, 'just as the moon [abandons] moonlight at dawn, so <s>Vaikuṇṭha</s> abandons <s>Śrī</s> for your sake' — this is <s>upamā</s> (simile). 'A ceaseless shower of nectar' — this is <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor).
<s>Bhāvika</s> (vivification):
Where past or future things are seen as if directly present,
and are most wondrous — that, through the fluency of expression, is <s>bhāvika</s> (vivification).

children.text:
sāṃpratikena pradhvaṃsābhāvenopalakṣyamāṇāḥ padārthāḥ bhūtāḥ, yathā idānīṃ yudhiṣṭhirādayaḥ /
ye tu sāpratikena prāgabhāvena upalakṣyante te bhāvinaḥ, yathā idānīṃ bhagavadavatāraḥ kalkī bhaviṣṇuyaśāḥ /
evamanantaropalakṣitāḥ bhūtā bhāvinaśca yer'thāste sāṃpratikapradhvaṃsābhāvaprāgabhāvaviviktatayā vartamānāyamānāḥ pratyakṣā iva yatra dṛśyante tadbhāvikaṃ nāmālaṅkāro bhavet /
atra heturvācāmanākulatā arthānāṃ cātyadbhutatvam /
taduktam---vācāmanākulyeneti /
atyadbhutā iti ca /
tatra vācāmanākulatā vyastasaṃbandharahitalokaprasiddhaśabdopanibandhājjhagityarthapratītikāritā /
tasyāṃ hi satyāṃ kaveḥ saṃbandhī yo bhāvaḥ
children.translated_text: Things that are past (<s>bhūta</s>) are those characterized by the absence-after-destruction (<s>pradhvaṃsābhāva</s>) indicated by the present, such as <s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s> and others at the present time. Those that are future (<s>bhāvinaḥ</s>) are those characterized by the prior-absence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) indicated by the present, such as the Blessed One's <s>Kalki</s> incarnation, <s>Bhaviṣṇuyaśas</s>, at the present time. Thus, when things that are past or future — characterized by the immediately indicated absence-after-destruction and prior-absence — being experienced as present, are seen as if directly perceived (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), that is the ornament called <s>bhāvika</s>. The cause here is the fluency of expression and the wondrous nature of the things. As stated: 'through the fluency of expression' and 'most wondrous.' Therein, the fluency of expression is the capacity to produce an instantaneous comprehension of meaning, arising from the binding together of commonly known words free from convoluted connections. When that obtains, the emotional state (<s>bhāva</s>) that belongs to the poet —

children.text:
āśrayaḥ śṛṅgārādirasasaṃvalitacaturvargopāyabhūtaviśiṣṭārthollekhī sa kavinaiva sahṛdayaiḥ śrotṛbhiḥ svābhiprāye 'bhedena tattatkāvyapratibimbitarūpatayā sākṣātkriyate /
śrotṛṇāmapi hi tathāvidhasvacchaśabdānubhavadrāvitāntarātmanāṃ sahṛdayānāṃ svābhiprāyapratimudrā tatra saṃkrāmati /
ataḥ kaveryo 'sāvabhiprāyastadgocarīkṛtā bhūtā bhāvino 'pi padārthastatra sahṛdayaiḥ śrotṛbhiḥ svābhiprāyābhedena pratyakṣā iva dṛśyante /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the inner disposition of the poet and the past and future objects that have been brought within its scope are seen by the sympathetic listeners as if directly present, through the non-difference from their own inner disposition.

children.text: yathā cātra śabdagatamanākulatvamanantaroktena prakāreṇa hetustathārthagatamapi citrodāttārthopanibandhahetukamatyadbhutatvaṃ draṣṭavyam /
children.translated_text: And just as the fluency pertaining to words is a cause in the manner just stated, so too the wondrousness pertaining to meaning, caused by the binding together of marvelous and sublime content, should be understood [as a cause].
As stated by <s>Bhāmaha</s> in the introduction to <s>bhāvika</s>: 'The wondrousness of marvelous and sublime content, self-enacted quality in narrative,
and the fluency of words — these they declare to be its causes.'

the repository that delineates the distinguished meanings that serve as means for the four aims of human life (<s>caturvarga</s>) suffused with <s>śṛṅgāra</s> and the other <s>rasas</s> — is directly experienced by the sympathetic listeners (<s>sahṛdaya</s>) as identical with their own inner disposition, reflected as it were in the mirror of the poetry. For even for the listeners, the sympathetic ones whose inner selves are melted by the experience of such lucid words, the seal of their own inner disposition is transmitted there.

children.text:
svabhinītatetyabhinayādidvāreṇa śṛṅgārādirasasaṃvalitatvaṃ caturvargopāyasyoktam /
tadevamevaṃvidhahetunibandhanaṃ kaviśrotṛbhāvadvitayasaṃmīlanātmakaṃ bhāvikaṃ draṣṭavyam /
children.translated_text: 'Self-enacted' (<s>svabhinītatā</s>) means the suffusion with <s>śṛṅgāra</s> and other <s>rasas</s> through the medium of dramatic enactment (<s>abhinaya</s>) and the like, which serves as means for the four aims of life. Thus, <s>bhāvika</s> should be seen as grounded in such causes and consisting in the merging of the two states — that of the poet and that of the listener.

children.text:
ata eva cātra kavisaṃbandhino bhāvasya śrotṛbhāvābhedādhyavasitasya puraḥ--sphuradrūpasya vidyamānatvādbhāvikavyapadeśaḥ bhāvo 'smin vidyate iti bhāvikam /
tadāhuḥ---"rasollāsī kaverātmā svacche śabdārthadarpaṇo /
mādhuryaujoyutaprauḍhe prativindya prakāśate /
saṃpītasvacchaśabdārthadrāvitābhyantarastataḥ /
śrotā tatsāmyataḥ puṣṭiṃ caturvarge parāṃ vrajet"iti /
svaccha iti prasādaguṇo 'bhihitaḥ /
prauḍha caturvarge parāṃ vrajet"iti /
svaccha iti prasādaguṇo 'bhihitaḥ /
prauḍha iti tu sālaṅkāratā /
saṃpītau samyagāsvāditau /
tatsāmyata iti svabhiprāyābhedena kavigatasyābhiprāyasyādhyavasānādityarthaḥ /
tasyodāharaṇam----
children.translated_text: For this very reason, the designation '<s>bhāvika</s>' [applies] because the emotional state belonging to the poet, determined as non-different from the listener's state, exists as a form that shines forth directly — <s>bhāva</s> (emotional state) exists in this, therefore it is <s>bhāvika</s>. Thus they say: 'The soul of the poet, overflowing with <s>rasa</s>, in the clear mirror of word and meaning, replete with sweetness (<s>mādhurya</s>), vigor (<s>ojas</s>), and mature grandeur (<s>prauḍhi</s>), manifests [itself] upon encountering [the listener]. Then the listener, having fully savored the clear words and meanings, his inner self melted thereby, attains through similarity to that [poet's state] the supreme nourishment in the four aims of life.' 'Clear' (<s>svaccha</s>) indicates the quality of lucidity (<s>prasāda</s>). 'Mature' (<s>prauḍha</s>) indicates the quality of being ornamented. 'Fully savored' (<s>saṃpīta</s>) means thoroughly relished. 'Through similarity to that' (<s>tatsāmyataḥ</s>) means through the determination of the poet's inner disposition as non-different [from one's own]. Its example:
You cause both pain and delight, O one with unadorned eyes,
when beheld in this form adorned with manifold ornaments.

children.text:
atrābharaṇocitamūrtitve 'pi nirañjanavilocanatvopalakṣitādābharaṇatyāgātpīḍā /
sahajasaundaryanirbharatvena tu ābharaṇasaṃpādyāyāḥ śobhāyāḥ paridṛśyamānatvātprītiḥ /
tenātra sāṃpratikapradhvaṃsābhāvopalakṣitatvādbhūṣaṇasaṃbandho vyatito 'pyadbhuto yo 'sau vapuḥprakarṣastadvaśena pratyatra iva kavinopanibaddhaḥ /
tathaiva cāsau sahṛdayānāṃ camatkāramāvahati /
saṃtatamutkṛṣṭatayā vaicitryeṇa īkṣaṇīyā ābharaṇaśobhā yasyāmiti bahuvrīhiḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, though she has a form suitable for ornaments, the pain arises from the abandonment of ornaments indicated by her having unadorned eyes. But the delight arises from the fact that, due to the fullness of her natural beauty, the splendor that ornaments would produce is [already] perceived. Therefore, here, because the connection with ornaments is characterized by absence-after-destruction indicated by the present — though passed — the wondrous excellence of her body is bound by the poet as if directly present through the force of that [excellence]. And in just that way, it produces aesthetic wonder (<s>camatkāra</s>) in the sympathetic [listeners]. 'Whose ornamental splendor is continuously worth beholding in its excellence and variety' — this is a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound.
<s>Kāvyaliṅga</s> (poetic reason):
When one thing that is heard comes to serve as the cause for the recollection or experience of another —
that is called <s>kāvyaliṅga</s> (poetic reason).

children.text:
yatra ekaṃ vastu śrutaṃ sadvastvantaraṃ smārayati anubhāvayati vā tatra kāvyaliṅgaṃ nāmālaṅkāraḥ /
pakṣadharmatvānvayavyatirekānusaraṇagarbhatayā yathā tārkikaprasiddhā hetavo lokaprasiddhavastuviṣayatvenopanibadhyamānā vairasyamāvahanti na tathā kāvyehetuḥ atiśayena sarveṣāṃ janānāṃ yosau hṛdayasaṃvādīsarasaḥ padārthastanniṣṭhatayā upanibadhyamānatvāt /
ataḥ kāvyaliṅgamiti kāvyagrahaṇamupāttam /
na khalu tacchāstraliṅgaṃ kiṃ tarhi kāvyaliṅgamiti kāvyagrahaṇena pratipādyate /
children.translated_text: Where one object that is heard causes the recollection or experience of another object — there is the ornament called <s>kāvyaliṅga</s>. Just as reasons well-known to logicians, being bound with respect to commonly known objects, along with the embedded following of the property-of-the-subject (<s>pakṣadharmatva</s>) and positive-and-negative concomitance (<s>anvayavyatireka</s>), produce distaste — the poetic reason does not do so in the same way, because it is bound with respect to that object which is in consonance with the hearts of all people, that supremely delightful thing. Therefore the word '<s>kāvya</s>' (poetic) is included [in the name] <s>kāvyaliṅga</s>. It is not a reason of the <s>śāstras</s> (sciences), but rather a poetic reason — this is what is conveyed by the word '<s>kāvya</s>.'

children.text:
nanu kāvyagrahaṇena kathaṃ kāvyasya sarasapadārthaniṣṭhatopadarśyate /
kāvyasya sarasatvāt /
kāvyaṃ khalu guṇasaṃskṛtaśabdārthaśarīratvāt sarasameva bhavati, na tu nīrasam /
tathāhi---guṇāḥ kāvyasya mādhuryaujaḥprasādalakṣaṇāḥ /
tatra mādhuryamāhlādakatvam, ojo gāḍhatā, prasādastvavyavadhānena
children.translated_text: Now, [question:] how does the word '<s>kāvya</s>' indicate that poetry is grounded in delightful objects? Because poetry is itself delightful. Poetry indeed is delightful and not insipid, because its body consists of words and meanings refined by <s>guṇas</s> (qualities). For thus: the <s>guṇas</s> of poetry are characterized as <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness), <s>ojas</s> (vigor), and <s>prasāda</s> (lucidity). Therein, <s>mādhurya</s> is the quality of producing delight; <s>ojas</s> is intensity; <s>prasāda</s> is

children.text:
rasābhivyaktyanuguṇatā /
tadeteṣāṃ trayāṇāṃ guṇānāṃ madhyātprasādasya prādhānyam /
mādhuryaujasostu tattadrasābhivyaktyānuguṇyena tāratamyenāvasthitayoḥ prasāda eva sopayogatā /
evaṃ ca tatra tadrasānuguṇyena mādhuryaujobhyāṃ tāratamyenāvasthitābhyāṃ upakṛto yo 'sau prasādātmā rasānāmavyavadhānena pratītiheturguṇastadupetaśabdārthaśarīratvena kāvyasyāvasthānātsarasataiva bhavati, na tu nīrasatā /
yadyevamidānīṃ guṇaireva kṛtakṛtyatvātkāvyasyālaṅkārāṇāṃ tatra nirupayogatā prāpnoti /
naivaṃ guṇāhitaśobhe kāvye alaṅkārāṇāṃ śobhātaśayavidhāyitvāllaukikālaṅkāravat /
yathāhi laukikānāmalaṅkārāṇāṃ guṇasaṃskṛte yuvativapuṣi nibadhyamānānāmalaṅkāratā evaṃ kāvyālaṅkārāṇāmapi draṣṭavyam /
children.translated_text: the suitability for the unobstructed manifestation of <s>rasa</s>. Among these three <s>guṇas</s>, <s>prasāda</s> has primacy. <s>Mādhurya</s> and <s>ojas</s>, being established in varying degrees according to the suitability for the manifestation of each particular <s>rasa</s>, have their utility only within <s>prasāda</s> itself. Thus, <s>prasāda</s> — that quality which causes the unobstructed apprehension of <s>rasas</s>, assisted by <s>mādhurya</s> and <s>ojas</s> established in varying degrees according to the suitability for each <s>rasa</s> — because poetry abides by having a body of words and meanings endowed with that [<s>prasāda</s>], it is delightful and not insipid. If that is so, then since poetry has already achieved its purpose through <s>guṇas</s> alone, the ornaments (<s>alaṅkāras</s>) would be useless therein. Not so — for in poetry whose beauty is established by <s>guṇas</s>, the ornaments serve to produce an excess of beauty, like worldly ornaments. For just as worldly ornaments produce their ornamental effect when bound upon a youthful body refined by [natural] qualities, so too should it be understood for poetic ornaments.

children.text:
nanu nirguṇe 'pi kāvye alaṅkārāṇāṃ guṇavacchobhāvidhāyitvaṃ kasmānneṣyate /
aparadṛṣṭatvāt /
na khalu nirguṇe kāvye nibadhyamānānāmalaṅkārāṇāṃ jaradyoṣidalaṅkāravacchobhāvidhāyitvaṃ dṛśyate /
children.translated_text: Now, [objection:] why is it not accepted that ornaments produce beauty, like <s>guṇas</s>, even in poetry devoid of <s>guṇas</s>? Because this is not observed. For ornaments, when bound in poetry devoid of <s>guṇas</s>, are not seen to produce beauty, like ornaments on an old woman.

children.text:
tathāhi----
jaradyoṣityalaṅkārāṃ nibadhyamānā na tasyāḥ śobhāṃ hīyate /
tathāhi---jaradyoṣityalaṅkārā nibadhyamānā na tasyāḥ śobhāṃ kurvanti, pratyuta tasyāṃ nibadhyamānānāṃ teṣāmātmīyameva saubhāgyaṃ hīyate /
children.translated_text: For thus: ornaments bound upon an old woman do not produce beauty for her; on the contrary, when bound upon her, their own charm is diminished.

children.text: tathā kāvyālaṅkārāṇāmapi nirguṇe kāvye nibadhyamānānāṃ kāvyaśobhāhetutvābhāvaḥ svaśobhāhāniśca bhavati /
children.translated_text: Likewise, poetic ornaments too, when bound in poetry devoid of <s>guṇas</s>, fail to cause the beauty of the poetry, and their own beauty is also diminished.

children.text: yadavocadbhaṭṭavāmanaḥ---"yuvateriva rūpamaṅga kāvyaṃ svadate śuddhaguṇaṃ tadapyatīva /
children.translated_text: As <s>Bhaṭṭa Vāmana</s> said: 'Like the form of a young woman, O dear one, poetry that possesses pure <s>guṇas</s> is indeed supremely relished,
all the more when graced with constant intimacy produced by the fancies of varied ornamental embellishments.
For thus: ornaments bound upon an old woman do not diminish her beauty —

children.text: yadi bhavati vacaścyutaṃ guṇebhyo vapuriva yauvanavandhyamaṅganāyāḥ /
children.translated_text: But if speech is bereft of <s>guṇas</s>, like the body of a woman barren of youth,
even ornaments that are pleasing to people inevitably partake of wretchedness.'

children.text:
"iti /
aṅgaśabda iṣṭāmantraṇe /
śuddhaguṇatvātsvadamānaṃ sadalaṅkāravikalpakalpanābhirvihitaparicayamatiśayena svadate iti saṃbandhaḥ /
ata evālaṅkārāṇaāmanityatā /
guṇarahitaṃ hi kāvyamakāvyameva bhavati, na tvalaṅkārarahitam /
alaṅkārāṇāṃ guṇorahitaṃ hi kāvyamakāvyameva bhavati, na tavalaṅkārarahitam /
alaṅkārāṇāṃ guṇopajanitaśobhe kāvye śobhātiśayavidhāyitvāt /
taduktam----
"kāvyaśobhāyāḥ kartāro dharmā guṇāḥ /
tadatiśayahetavastvalaṅkārāḥ /
pūrve nityāḥ /

children.translated_text: Thus.
'The former' means the <s>guṇas</s>.

children.text: lakṣye ca alaṅkārarahitamapi kevalaguṇasaṃskriyamāṇaśabdārthaśarīraṃ kāvyaṃ dṛśyate, yathā amarukasya kaveranibaddhaśṛṅgārarasasyandī ślokaḥ---"kathamapi kṛtapratyāpattau priye skhalitottare virahakṛśayā kṛtvā vyājaprakalpatamaśrutam /
children.translated_text: And in actual examples, poetry that is devoid of ornaments but has a body of words and meanings refined solely by <s>guṇas</s> is observed — such as the verse of the poet <s>Amaru</s>, overflowing with the <s>śṛṅgāra</s> <s>rasa</s> (erotic sentiment) that he composed: 'When the beloved, stammering in his reply, somehow manages to make amends, she, emaciated by separation, fabricating a feigned [posture of] not having heard —
with the anxious confusion of inadvertently letting [the words] reach the ears of her impatient friend, with averted gaze, in the empty house, then she sighed.'

Thus. The word '<s>aṅga</s>' is an affectionate mode of address. The connection is: being relished because of possessing pure <s>guṇas</s>, it is supremely relished [when] made intimate by the fancies of varied ornamental embellishments. For this very reason, ornaments are non-permanent [components]. For poetry devoid of <s>guṇas</s> is simply non-poetry, but poetry devoid of ornaments [is still poetry]. Because ornaments serve to produce an excess of beauty in poetry whose beauty has been generated by <s>guṇas</s>. As stated: 'The properties (<s>dharmas</s>) that create the beauty of poetry are <s>guṇas</s>. The causes of its excess are <s>alaṅkāras</s>. The former are permanent.

children.text:
"iti /
na khalvatrārthalaṅkāraḥ kaścitparidṛśyate /
atha mādhuryaujobhyāṃ paribṛṃhatasya prasādasya vidyamānatvātkāvyarūpatā /
children.translated_text: Thus. Indeed no ornament of meaning (<s>arthālaṅkāra</s>) whatsoever is observed here. Yet, because of the presence of <s>prasāda</s> nourished by <s>mādhurya</s> and <s>ojas</s>, it has the nature of poetry.

children.text:
nanu cātrāpi īrṣyāvipralambhavirahavipralambhaśṛṅgārābhyāṃ svatirodhānenopakṛtaḥ saṃbhogaśṛṅgāro nāyikāniṣṭho nibaddhastadyogācca rasavattvamalaṃ bhaviṣyati /
tathāhi 'kathamapi kṛtapratyāpattau priye'ityatra bhāge virahavipralambhapūrvakaḥ priyatamacittasāṃmukhyātmā saṃbhogaśṛṅgāraḥ sūcitaḥ /
ssvalitottara iti tu saṃjātagotraskhalitatvātpreyaso nāyikāyā īrṣyāvipralambhaśṛṃgāro nibaddhaḥ /
punaśca virahakṛśayetyādibhistribhiḥ pādairavahitthena bhāvena nāyikādhāramīrṣyā vipralambhaśṛṅgāraṃ pracchādya saṃbhogaśṛṅgāreṇa cittollāsasūcitena vākyārthasamāptiḥ kṛtā /
tathā hi---virahakṛśetyādinā pādena nāyikāgato manyuravacchādyopadarśitaḥ /
asahanasakhītyādinā tu gotraskhalitasya sakhīśrotraprāptiṃ virahavipralambhakāraṇatvenāśaṅkya dṛṣṭiparāvṛttyā sakhījanaśūnye gṛhe paridṛṣṭe yattannayakayā samullasitaṃ tadupanibandhātsaṃbhogaśṛṅgāreṇa vākyārtho nirvāhitaḥ /
tadevamatra saṃbhogasya vapralambhavādhena labdhapadabandhasyopanibandhādrasavattvamalaṅkāraḥ /
tatkathamatra niralaṅkāratoktā /
ucyate /
na khalu kāvyasya rasānāṃ vālaṅkāryālaṅkārabhāvaḥ, kintu ātmaśarīrabhāvaḥ /
rasā hi kāvayasyātmatvena avasthitāḥ, śabdārthau ca śarīrarūpatayā /
yathā hyātmādhiṣṭhitaṃ śarīraṃ jīvatīti vyapadiśyate tathā rasādhiṣṭhitasya kāvyasya jīvadrūpatayā vyapadeśaḥ kriyate /
tasmādrasānāṃ kāvyaśarīrabhūtaśabdārthaviṣayatayātmatvenāvasthānaṃ, natvalaṅkāratayā /
rasābhivyaktiśca yathāyogaṃ mādhuryaujobhyāṃ tāratamyenāvasthitābhyāmupabṛṃhito yo 'sau prasādātmā guṇastena kriyate /
ato 'tra vipralambhaśṛṅgāropakṛtasya saṃbhogaśṛṅgārasya saguṇakāvyātmatvenāvasthānaṃ, na tu kāvyaṃ prati alaṅkāratayeti yuktamidamuktaṃ niralaṅkāramapi kāvyaṃ saguṇaṃ dṛśyate iti /
children.translated_text: Therefore, here the <s>saṃbhogaśṛṅgāra</s> assisted by <s>vipralambhaśṛṅgāra</s> abides as the self of poetry endowed with qualities — not as an ornament to the poetry. Thus it is proper that it was said: 'Poetry, even without ornaments, is seen as endowed with qualities.'

children.text: evaṃ rasāntareṣu bhāveṣu rasabhāvābhāseṣu tatpraśameṣu ca vācyam /
children.translated_text: In the same way, this should be stated with respect to other <s>rasas</s>, <s>bhāvas</s> (emotions), semblances of <s>rasa</s> and <s>bhāva</s> (<s>rasabhāvābhāsa</s>), and their subsidence (<s>praśama</s>).
Therefore they say: "Since poetry presided over by <s>rasa</s> and the like is designated as having a living form,
the selfhood of <s>rasa</s> and the like with respect to poetry is established."

Now, here too, since the <s>saṃbhogaśṛṅgāra</s> (love-in-union) that is benefited by <s>īrṣyāvipralambha</s> (love-in-separation due to jealousy) and <s>virahavipralambhaśṛṅgāra</s> (love-in-separation due to absence) through their self-concealment is bound as pertaining to the heroine — and since there is the connection with that [rasa] — the quality of being <s>rasavat</s> (endowed with rasa) will certainly obtain. Thus, in the portion 'when the beloved, having been brought back with great difficulty' — there the <s>saṃbhogaśṛṅgāra</s>, preceded by <s>virahavipralambha</s>, characterized by the turning of the beloved's mind [toward the heroine], is suggested. In 'having a misstep as the sequel' — since the hero's misstep regarding his lineage-name has occurred — the <s>īrṣyāvipralambhaśṛṅgāra</s> of the heroine is bound. And again, by the three feet beginning with 'emaciated by separation' etc., through the concealing sentiment (<s>avahittha bhāva</s>), the <s>īrṣyāvipralambhaśṛṅgāra</s> residing in the heroine is hidden, and the sentence-meaning is concluded with the <s>saṃbhogaśṛṅgāra</s> suggested by the delight of the heart. Thus — by the foot beginning with 'emaciated by separation' etc., the anger residing in the heroine is shown in a concealed manner. By 'unable to bear, the friend' etc., having suspected that the misstep regarding the lineage-name reaching the friend's ear might be a cause for <s>virahavipralambha</s>, and having turned her gaze and observed that the house is empty of friends — what was then joyfully displayed by the hero — through its binding, the sentence-meaning is concluded with <s>saṃbhogaśṛṅgāra</s>. Thus, here the binding of <s>saṃbhoga</s> (love-in-union), which has obtained its foothold through the impediment of <s>vipralambha</s> (love-in-separation), constitutes the ornament of being <s>rasavat</s>. How then can it be said that there is no ornament here? The answer is: the relationship between poetry and <s>rasas</s> is not that of what is to be ornamented and the ornament, but rather that of self and body. The <s>rasas</s> abide as the self (<s>ātman</s>) of poetry, while word and meaning [abide] in the form of the body. Just as a body presided over by the self is designated as 'living,' so too poetry presided over by <s>rasa</s> is designated as having a living form. Therefore, the <s>rasas</s>, having as their domain the word and meaning that constitute the body of poetry, abide as its self — not as its ornament. And the manifestation of <s>rasa</s> is accomplished by the quality called <s>prasāda</s> (lucidity), which is nourished by <s>mādhurya</s> (sweetness) and <s>ojas</s> (vigor), present in varying degrees as appropriate.
Thus.

children.text:
yattu rasādīnāṃ pūrvamalaṅkāratvamuktaṃ tadevaṃvidhabhedāvivakṣayā /
tadevaṃ guṇasaṃskṛtaśabdārthaśarīratvātsarasameva kāvyam /
yadyevaṃ guṇaśūnyatvānnīrase
children.translated_text: The earlier statement that <s>rasa</s> and the like are ornaments was made without intending such a distinction. In this way, poetry is always endowed with <s>rasa</s>, because it has word-and-meaning as its body, refined by qualities (<s>guṇa</s>). If so, then because of being devoid of qualities and being without <s>rasa</s>,

children.text: vyākaraṇādau bharatādau ca kāvyavyapadeśo na prāptaḥ /
children.translated_text: the designation of 'poetry' is not obtained for grammar and <s>Bharata</s>'s [science of dramaturgy] and the like.
And therefore: "That which narrates the conduct of gods and the like, and that which has a subject that is forced [upon it],
and that which rests upon art or upon science — [poetry] is again divided fourfold."

children.text:
"iti bhāmahoditaṃ virudhyate, atra hi kalāśrayaśabdena bharatādyabhihitam /
śāstrāśrayaśabdena ca vyākaraṇādi /
ato vaktavyametatkathaṃ tatra kāvyavyapadeśaḥ iti /
ucyate /
mukhyayā tāvadvṛttyā guṇasaṃskṛtaśabdārthaśarīrameva kāvyam /
guṇarahitaśabdārthaśarīre tu kvāyamātre kāvyaśabdasya kāvyasādṛśyādupacārātprayogo bhaviṣyati /
uktaṃ ca---"kāvyaśabdo 'yaṃ guṇālaṅkārasaṃskṛtayoḥ śabdārthayorvarte, bhaktyā tu śabdārthamātravacano 'tra gṛhte"iti /
bhaktyeti upacāreṇetyarthaḥ /
tadevaṃ guṇasaṃskṛtaśabdārthaśarīratvātkāvyasya sarasatvamiti /
tadviśiṣṭaṃ kāvyaliṅgaṃ
children.translated_text: This statement by <s>Bhāmaha</s> is contradicted, for here by the word 'art-based' is meant what is taught by <s>Bharata</s> and others, and by the word 'science-based,' grammar and the like. Therefore it must be stated: how is the designation of 'poetry' [applied] there? The answer is: in the primary sense, poetry is indeed that whose body is word-and-meaning refined by qualities. But for mere word-and-meaning-body that is devoid of qualities, the use of the word 'poetry' will be through figurative extension (<s>upacāra</s>), based on similarity to poetry. As stated: 'This word "poetry" applies to word and meaning that are refined by qualities and ornaments; but in a secondary sense (<s>bhakti</s>), it is taken as denoting mere word and meaning here.' '<s>Bhakti</s>' means 'through figurative extension (<s>upacāra</s>).' Thus, poetry's being endowed with <s>rasa</s> is because of having as its body word-and-meaning refined by qualities. That which is distinguished [by rasa] is <s>kāvyaliṅga</s> (poetic mark/reason) —

children.text:
sarasapadārthaniṣṭhameva bhavatiṣa na tu nīrasavastumātraniṣṭhaṃ śāstraliṅgavadityupapannam /
tārkikāṇāṃ ca hetuvyāpāre dvaividhyam /
kecitkhalu tārkakā vyāptigrahaṇakāle yadanubhūtaṃ vyāpakaṃ vahnyādivastu dhūmādervyāpyasya tatsmaraṇamātre dhūmādihetudarśanaprabuddhasaṃskārāṇāṃ puruṣāṇāṃ hetuvyāpāraṃ manyante /
apare tu vahnyādīnāṃ parvatādidharmaviśeṣasaṃbandhasya pūrvamagṛhītasya dhūmādihetuvyāpārasāmarthyena idānīmeva avaseyatvālliṅgasāmarthyālliṅgyanubhavasyaiva utpattimāhuḥ /
tadidamuktaṃ smṛteranubhavasya veti /
tasyodāharaṇam----
children.translated_text: it pertains only to content endowed with <s>rasa</s>, not to mere <s>rasa</s>-less subject matter like a logical mark (<s>śāstraliṅga</s>). This is established. Among logicians, there is a twofold [view] regarding the operation of the inferential mark (<s>hetu</s>). Some logicians hold that the operation of the inferential mark consists in the mere recollection — for persons whose latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) are awakened by seeing the inferential mark such as smoke — of the pervading entity such as fire etc. that was experienced at the time of grasping the invariable concomitance (<s>vyāpti</s>). Others, however, say that since the connection of fire etc. as a specific property of a mountain etc. was not previously grasped, and is now to be determined only through the power of the operation of the inferential mark such as smoke, it is the experience of the inferable (<s>liṅgya</s>) itself that is newly produced through the power of the mark (<s>liṅga</s>). This is what is meant by 'whether through recollection or through experience.' An illustration of that —
"This shadow of the radiance of your emaciated limbs is somewhat dim,
revealing the places for arranging ornaments — it pains me." [UKss 6.*8]

children.text: atra vibhūṣaṇavinyāsāspadabhūtā ye kaṇṭhādayastadavaśiṣṭānāmaṅgānāṃ yāsau kāntiḥ dīptiḥ tasyā anujjvalā malinā yāsau chāyā śobhā sā liṅgaṃ, tatsāmarthyācca bhūṣāvinyāsapradeśānāṃ bhūṣaṇasaṃbandho 'tīto 'numīyate /
children.translated_text: Here, the radiance (<s>kānti</s>) — the luster — of the limbs remaining after the [removal of ornaments from] the throat etc. that served as sites for arranging ornaments: the shadow (<s>chāyā</s>), the beauty, of that [radiance] which is dim — that is the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>); and through its power, the past connection of ornaments with the places for arranging ornaments is inferred.
Therefore that is <s>kāvyaliṅga</s> (poetic inferential mark).
<s>Kāvyadṛṣṭānta</s> (poetic example) —
A lucid illustration that is a reflection of the intended meaning,
free of words such as 'as if' (<s>yathā</s>, <s>iva</s>) — the wise call that a [poetic] example. [UKss 6.8]

children.text: iṣṭasya prākaraṇikatayā pratipādayitumabhimatasyārthasya yatra vispaṣṭatayā pratibimbaṃ sadṛśa vastu nidarśyate tatra kāvyadṛṣṭānto nāmālaṅkāraḥ /
children.translated_text: Where, for an intended meaning that is to be established as the primary subject, a similar entity is shown clearly as a reflection — there the ornament called <s>kāvyadṛṣṭānta</s> [obtains].

children.text:
nanu "kopādekatarāghātanipatanmattadantinaḥ /
harerhariṇayuddheṣu kiyānvyākṣepavistaraḥ"ityevamādāvapi aprastutapraśaṃsāyāmiṣṭārthapratibimbanidarśanaṃ vidyate /
tathāhi---atra rāmadevasya mārīcavadhe vyāpāro nirāyāso hariṇahananodyogikasarikiśorapratibimbitatvena nidarśitaḥ /
ato 'trāpi dṛṣṭāntatāprasaṅgaḥ /
naitat /
yata etadarthameva vispaṣṭagrahaṇamupāttam /
atra hi pratibambādeva bimbasyonnayanādvispaṣṭarūpatayā iṣṭasyārthasya pratibimbanidarśanaṃ nāsti /
yatra tu iṣṭamarthaṃ svakaṇṭhenopādāya tasya pratibimbamupadarśyate tatra dṛṣṭāntatvam /
ato nātavyāptiḥ /
upamādāvapyetvaṃvidhasya rūpasya saṃbhava iti tannirākaraṇārthamuktam---yathevādipadaiḥ śūnyamiti /
ādigrahaṇenātra sādhāraṇadharmasyāpi parigrahaḥ /
tasyodāharaṇam----
children.translated_text: Now, even in [verses like] 'an enraged elephant striking with one tusk, falling upon — how great is the extent of <s>Hari</s>'s exertion in battles with deer-like [enemies]?' and so forth, in the case of <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the unintended subject) too, there is the illustration of a reflection of the intended meaning. Thus, here <s>Rāmadeva</s>'s effortless exertion in the killing of <s>Mārīca</s> is shown through being reflected in a young lion's endeavor to kill a deer. Therefore, the unwanted consequence of [this being classified as] a poetic example would follow here too. This is not so. For it is precisely for this purpose that the word 'lucid' (<s>vispaṣṭa</s>) was adopted. Here, since the primary object is inferred from the reflection alone, the illustration of the intended meaning's reflection is not in a lucid form. But where the intended meaning is first stated in one's own words and then its reflection is shown — there the status of [poetic] example [obtains]. Therefore there is no over-extension. And to prevent the possibility of such a form occurring in <s>upamā</s> (simile) and the like, it is said: 'free of words such as <s>yathā</s> and <s>iva</s>.' By the word 'etc.' (<s>ādi</s>), the common property too is included. An illustration of that —
"Moreover, what is the point of much speaking? Go and obtain a husband!
Without reaching the ocean, what do the great rivers accomplish?" [UKss 6.*9]

children.text:
atra bhagavatīkartṛkāyā varaprāptermahānadīkartṛkā udanvatprārvispaṣṭatayā pratibimbatvenopanibaddhā /
ato dṛṣṭāntaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, the attainment of a husband by the Goddess as agent is bound as a reflection — in a lucid form — of the great rivers reaching the ocean as agent. Therefore this is a [poetic] example.
Thus, through groups of eight, six, three, seven, eleven, and six, in six chapters, forty-one ornaments have been demonstrated.

children.text:
nanu yatra kāvye sahṛdayahṛdayāhlādinaḥ pradhānabhūtasya svaśabvyāpārāspṛṣṭatvena pratīyamānaikarūpasyārthasya sadbhavastatra tathāvidhārthābhivyaktihetuḥ kāvyajīvatabhūtaḥ kaiścatsahṛdayairdhvanirnāma vyañjakatvabhedātmā kāvyadharmo 'bhihitaḥ /
sa kasmādiha nopadiṣṭaḥ /
ucyate /
eṣvevālaṅkāreṣvantarbhāvāt /
tathāhi---pratīyamānaikarūpasya vastutraividhyaṃ tairuktaṃ vastumātrālaṅkārarasādibhedena /
tatra vastumātraṃ tāvatpratīyate yathā---
children.translated_text: Now, where in poetry there exists a single-formed meaning that delights the hearts of the sensitive (<s>sahṛdaya</s>), that is primary, that is apprehended through suggestion untouched by the operation of [direct] words — there, some sensitive critics have declared a property of poetry called <s>dhvani</s> (resonance/suggestion), whose nature consists in the distinction of suggestive power, as the life-force of poetry. Why is it not taught here? The answer is: because it is subsumed within these very ornaments. Thus, the threefold nature of the single-formed entity that is suggested has been stated by them — distinguished as mere subject matter (<s>vastu</s>), ornament (<s>alaṃkāra</s>), and <s>rasa</s> etc. Among these, mere subject matter is suggested as in —
"By the very command given with the force of the discus-blow, he made
the love-festival of <s>Rāhu</s>'s women, barren of the sport of tight embraces, reduced to mere kissing."
Thus.

children.text:
atra hi rāhuvadhūratotsavasya yā cumbanamātreśeṣatā tatkarmakā cakrābhighātaprasabhājñākaraṇikā cakāreti karaṇalakṣaṇā kriyābhidhīyate /
sā
children.translated_text: Here, that the love-festival of <s>Rāhu</s>'s women has mere kissing as its remainder — the action of making, characterized by the agency of the command given with the force of the discus-blow, is stated with that as its object.

children.text:
caivaṃvidhā kāryabhūtatvātkāraṇamantareṇānupapadyamānā tathāvidhavairasyakāri rāhuśiraśchedalakṣaṇaṃ kāraṇaṃ nālaṅkārarūpaṃ, nāpi rasādirūpaṃ, api tu vastumātrarūpaṃ kalpayati /
ato 'tra vastumātrasyaivaṃvidhasya śabdavyāpārāspṛṣṭasya pratīyamānatā, tadviṣayasya ca kāvyadharmasya dhvananābhidhānasya vācyavācakavyāpāraśūnyāvagamanasvabhāvatvātparyāyoktālaṅkārasparś itvaṃ, taduktam----
"paryāyoktaṃ yadanyena"ityādi /
children.translated_text: And being of such nature — as an effect, being untenable without its cause — [this action] constructs a cause characterized by the cutting of <s>Rāhu</s>'s head, which produces such aversion; that cause is not in the form of an ornament, nor in the form of <s>rasa</s> and the like, but rather in the form of mere subject matter. Therefore, here the suggested nature of mere subject matter of such kind, untouched by the operation of words, [obtains]; and the poetry-property called <s>dhvani</s> (suggestion) pertaining to that domain — because of having the nature of comprehension devoid of the operation of the expressed and the expresser — has a connection with the ornament of <s>paryāyokta</s> (indirect expression). As stated: '<s>Paryāyokta</s> is that which [is expressed] by another [means]' and so forth.

children.text:
nanu paryāyoktaśabdena prakārāntareṇa ucyamāntvātpratīyamānaṃ vastu abhidhīyate /
tacceha pratīyamānaṃ
children.translated_text: Now, by the word <s>paryāyokta</s>, since it means 'being stated by another manner,' the suggested subject matter is referred to.

children.text:
pradhānatvādalaṅkāryatayā vaktuṃ yuktam, na tvalaṅkṛtikāraṇatayā /
ataḥ kathaṃ tasyālaṅkāravyapadeśaḥ /
ucyate /
pradhānamapi guṇānāṃ saundaryahetutvādalaṅkṛtau sādhanatvaṃ bhajati /
dṛśyate hi loke vyapadeśaḥ svāmyalaṅkaraṇakā bhṛtyā iti /
ato 'trāpi pratīyamānasya satyapi pradhānatve svaguṇabhūtavācyasaundaryasādhakatamatvādalaṅkāravyapadeśo na virudhyate /
yadi vā bhagavadvāsudevavartitayā yo 'sau vīraraso 'vagamyate tadapekṣayā tasya mukhyayaiva vṛttyā guṇabhūtatvādalaṅkāratā /
evamuttaratrāpi yathāsaṃbhavaṃ yojyam /
children.translated_text: And since that suggested [meaning] is primary, it is proper to speak of it as what is to be ornamented (<s>alaṃkārya</s>), not as the cause of ornamentation. Therefore, how can the designation of 'ornament' [apply to it]? The answer is: even what is primary takes on the role of instrumentality in ornamentation, because the qualities are causes of beauty. Indeed, in the world, the expression is observed: 'servants are the adornment of the master.' Therefore, here too, even though the suggested [meaning] is primary, since it is most effective in producing the beauty of the expressed meaning that constitutes its own quality — the designation of 'ornament' is not contradicted. Alternatively, the <s>vīrarasa</s> (heroic sentiment) that is comprehended with respect to the Lord <s>Vāsudeva</s>'s conduct — with respect to that [rasa], since [the suggested meaning] has the status of a quality in the primary sense — its ornament-status [follows]. In the same way, the subsequent [cases] too should be construed as appropriate.
"The clouds, dark with the luster of deep blue brilliance spread across the sky, with heaving rows of cranes,
the winds bearing drizzle, the arts of the joyous <s>kekā</s>-cries of the friends of the clouds [i.e., peacocks] —

children.text: kāmaṃ santu dṛḍhaṃ kaṭhorahṛdayo rāmo 'smi sarvaṃ sahe
children.translated_text: let them all be! I am <s>Rāma</s>, hard-hearted and firm, I endure everything;

children.text: vaidehī tu kathaṃ bhaviṣyati hahā hā devi dhīrā bhava" //
children.translated_text: but <s>Vaidehī</s> — how will she fare? Alas, alas! O lady, be steadfast!"

children.text:
ityevamādāvapi rāmādīnāṃ śabdānāmasādhāraṇarūpatayā rājyabhraṃśavanavāsasītāharaṇapitṛmaraṇādayo duḥkhaikahetavaḥ svārthasahacāriṇo vastumātrarūpā vyaṅgyadharmāstatpariṇatarūpatayā svārthasya pratītistadvetubhūtatvātparyāyoktālaṅkārasaṃsparśitaiva /
na khalu pade paryāyoktena bhavitavyamitīyaṃ rājñāmājñā sūtrakāravacanaṃ vā /
lakṣaṇayogādvi vibhaktarūpatāvasthāpyate /
atra ca paryāyoktalakṣaṇaṃ vidyate /

children.translated_text: because there exists a mode of comprehension whose nature is understanding devoid of the operation of the expressed and the expresser.
Therefore, how could the status of <s>paryāyokta</s> not obtain?
In the same way, in other cases too where mere subject matter is suggested, the status of <s>paryāyokta</s> should be stated.

children.text: tasmānna vastumātre pratīyamāne tadabhivyaktihetuḥ kāvyadharmo dhvanirnāmārthāntaram //
children.translated_text: Therefore, when mere subject matter is suggested, the poetry-property called <s>dhvani</s> (suggestion) — the cause of its manifestation — is not something separate [from the ornaments].

In [verses] such as this too, through the specific nature of words like '<s>Rāma</s>' etc., the suggested properties (<s>vyaṅgyadharma</s>) — the sole causes of suffering such as loss of kingdom, forest-exile, abduction of <s>Sītā</s>, death of the father, and the like — which are concomitants of their own meanings, in the form of mere subject matter: the cognition of their own meaning in the form of their result — because it is caused by those — has a connection with the ornament of <s>paryāyokta</s> (indirect expression). It is not the case that a royal command or an author's dictum says 'the word <s>paryāyokta</s> must apply [only in certain cases].' The [ornament's] distinct form is established through the fitness of its defining characteristics. And here the defining characteristic of <s>paryāyokta</s> is present,
As for ornaments, although —
"In this smiling face of yours, O one of trembling wide eyes,
whose mouth is filled with the splendor of charm pervading all directions —

children.text: kṣobhaṃ yadeti na manāgapi tena manye
children.translated_text: the fact that [the ocean] is not agitated in the slightest — by that I think
this ocean is quite clearly a mere body of water."

children.text:
ityādau pratīyamānaikarūpatā, tathāpyanantaroktalakṣaṇeṣvalaṅkāreṣu anupraveśo bhaviṣyati paryāyokte vā /
tathā hyatra śloke mukhyasya lāvaṇyakāntiparipūritadiṅbhukhasya vikasitahāsajyotsnasya saṃbodhanasāmarthyāvasitataralāyatākṣitvasya ca saṃnidhānājjalanidheḥ kṣobhamupapattimattvena saṃbhāvya tadbhāvo jāḍyasamūhāvacchāditasvabhāvatvādabhihitaḥ /
tathāvidhārthaparyālocanayā cātra mukhasya candreṇa rūpaṇā pratīyate /
candrasaṃnidhānājjalanidheḥ kṣobhasyotpādadarśanāt /
na ca yasyālaṅkārasya pratīyamānarūpatā tasyehālaṅkāratvaṃ kenacinnivāritamiti pratīyamānarūpatayā rūpakākhyo 'laṅkāro bhaviṣyati /
athavā paryāyoktyā rūpakasyātrāvasatatvātparyayoktamalaṅkāraḥ /
children.translated_text: In [verses] such as this there is a single-formed suggested nature; nevertheless, the entry [of the suggested meaning] will be into the ornaments described in the characteristics stated above, or into <s>paryāyokta</s>. For in this verse, because of the proximity of the primary subject — the face whose directional expanse is filled with the splendor of charm — having blossoming laughter-moonlight, and the trembling wide-eyedness ascertained through the power of the vocative: the agitation of the ocean, being apprehended as plausible, its non-occurrence is stated as having its nature concealed by the aggregation of dullness. Through the contemplation of such meaning, here the identification (<s>rūpaṇā</s>) of the face with the moon is suggested. Because agitation of the ocean is observed to occur when the moon is in proximity. And it is not the case that anyone has prohibited the ornament-status of that ornament whose nature is suggested. Therefore, the ornament called <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) will obtain in its suggested form. Alternatively, because <s>rūpaka</s> here rests upon <s>paryāyokti</s>, the ornament is <s>paryāyokta</s>.
"Three types of men gather the earth that has golden flowers:
the brave, the learned, and he who knows how to serve."

children.text:
ityādau tu śūrādibhiḥ saha suvarṇapuṣpapṛthivīkarmakasya cayanasyānupapadyamānānvayatvātsādṛśyasyānvayenopameyabhūtasya bahulābhatvasya tatsadṛśasya yā lakṣaṇā taddvāreṇa garbhīkṛtopamānopameyabhāvā asaṃbhavadvācyārthā nidarśanā draṣṭavyā /
yaduktam---"abhavanvastusaṃbandha"ityādi /
bhaṭṭavāmanena cātra vaktoktivyavahāraḥ pravartitaḥ /
yadavocat---"sādṛśyāllakṣaṇā vaktoktiri"ti /
children.translated_text: In [verses] such as this, however, since the connection of the gathering — whose object is the golden-flowered earth — with the brave and the like is untenable, through the connection of similarity, by means of the figurative usage (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) of that which is similar to the abundant [wealth] that is the <s>upameya</s> — thereby should be seen <s>nidarśanā</s> (illustration), which incorporates the <s>upamāna-upameya</s> relationship, and which has an impossible literal meaning. As stated: 'When there is no connection of real entities' and so forth. And <s>Bhaṭṭa Vāmana</s> has applied the designation of <s>vakrokti</s> (oblique expression) here. As he said: '<s>Lakṣaṇā</s> based on similarity is <s>vakrokti</s>.'
"Bow to the one who is the sole refuge of all, imperishable, lord of lords, master of intellects, <s>Hari</s>, <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>,
four-souled, actionless, destroyer of enemies, bearer of the discus."

children.text:
ityādāvapi śleṣaḥ /
tathā hyatra sarvaikaśaraṇamakṣayamityādīnāṃ śabdānāmarthabhedena bhinnatve sati yathāyogamekaprayatnoccāryāṇāmekapratayatnoccāryaśabdasadṛśānāṃ voccāraṇam /
ato virodhālaṅkārapratibhotpattiheturatra śleṣaḥ /
yaduktam---"ekaprayatnoccāryāṇām"ityādi /
children.translated_text: and so on — here too there is <s>śleṣa</s> (paronomasia). For here, the words '<s>sarvaikaśaraṇam</s>' (sole refuge of all), '<s>akṣayam</s>' (imperishable), and the like, despite having distinct meanings through semantic differentiation, are pronounced as if [they were] words pronounced with a single effort, or as words similar to those pronounced with a single effort. Therefore, the <s>śleṣa</s> here is the cause for the arising of the ornament of <s>virodha</s> (contradiction). As stated: 'of those pronounced with a single effort' and so forth.

children.text:
evamalaṅkārāntareṣvapi pratīyamāneṣu vācyam /
tenālaṅkāraniṣṭhasyāpi abhivyañjakatvasyokteṣvalaṅkāreṣvantarbhāvādavyāptyabhāvaḥ /
rasabhāvatadābhāsatatpraśamānāṃ tu
children.translated_text: In this way, the same should be stated when other ornaments too are suggested. Therefore, since the suggestive function (<s>vyañjakatva</s>) pertaining to ornaments is subsumed within the stated ornaments, there is no under-extension (<s>avyāpti</s>). But when <s>rasa</s>, <s>bhāva</s>, their semblances (<s>ābhāsa</s>), and their quiescence (<s>praśama</s>)
are suggested, an illustration [is as follows] —
"When the lapse in the family name entered the path of hearing, [she] who had come to the bed,
having meditated, agreed to undertake the turning-over [to the other side] once more.
Again, what was begun was carried out — but with a single loosely thrown arm-line,

children.text: tanvaṅgyā na tu pāritaḥ stanabharaḥ ṛṣṭuṃ priyasyorasaḥ" //
children.translated_text: the slender-limbed one did not allow her breast's weight to touch the chest of her beloved."
Thus.

children.text:
tathā hi--atra gotraskhalitasya śrutipathaprāpterīrṣyāvipralambhaśṛṅgāro nāyikāyāḥ saṃmukhībhūto 'pi saṃbhogaśṛṅgāreṇa svahetusāmagryapratilabdhaprakarṣeṇa tirodhāya pradarśitaḥ /
nirdhyātaṃ parivartanamityādinā hi yathākramamīrṣyāvipralambhaśṛṅgārānubhāvasya parivartanasya darśanaprārthanādhyavasāyānuṣṭhānātmikāścatasro 'vasthāḥ saṃbhogaśṛṅgāramantharīkṛtasvasvabhāvatvenopavarṇitāḥ /
punaśca saṃbhogaśṛṅgāreṇa vākyārtho nirvāhito 'na tu pāritaḥ'ityādinā /
ato 'tra saṃbhogaśṛṅgārasyerṣyāvipralambhaśṛṅgāratirodhānahetoḥ pratīyamānatā /
tatra ca pūrvaṃ rasavattvalakṣaṇo 'laṅkāraḥ pratipādito 'rasavaddarśita'ityādinā /
evaṃ rasāntareṣvapi vācyam /
children.translated_text: For here, the <s>īrṣyāvipralambhaśṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment in the mode of love-in-separation through jealousy) of the heroine, who heard the slip of another's name — though directly confronted [by her] — is shown as concealed by <s>saṃbhogaśṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment in the mode of union), which has attained full intensity through the completeness of its own causal conditions. For by 'she meditated, the turning-over' and so forth, the four stages — seeing, desiring, resolving, and executing — of the turning-over (which is the <s>anubhāva</s>, i.e., consequent behavior, of the <s>īrṣyāvipralambhaśṛṅgāra</s>) are successively described as having their own natures retarded by the <s>saṃbhogaśṛṅgāra</s>. And furthermore, the sentence-meaning is concluded by the <s>saṃbhogaśṛṅgāra</s> through 'but did not allow' and so forth. Therefore here, the <s>saṃbhogaśṛṅgāra</s>, which is the cause of concealing the <s>īrṣyāvipralambhaśṛṅgāra</s>, has the status of being suggested. And therein, the ornament called <s>rasavattva</s> (the quality of being replete with <s>rasa</s>) has been previously established by the passage 'shown as <s>rasavat</s>' and so forth. The same should be stated regarding other <s>rasas</s> as well.

children.text:
yatrāpi bhāvastathā rasabhāvābhāsā rasabhāvatadābhāsapraśamāśca pratīyamānāstatrāpi yathākramaṃ preyasvadūrjasvitsamāhitalakṣaṇālaṅkārayogo vācyaḥ /
evametatpradhānabhūteṣu rasādiṣūktam /
guṇabhūteṣvapi ca raseṣūdāttālaṅkāraḥ pratipāditaḥ 'caritaṃ ca mahātmanām'ityādinā /
ataśca rasādiṣvabhivyañjakatvasya nārthāntaratā /
evaṃ ca trividhe 'pi pratīyamāner'the yacchaṣṭhānāṃ vyañjakatvamanantaropavarṇiteṣūdāharaṇeṣu ṣaṭūprakāratayopadarśitaṃ tasyokteṣvevālaṅkāreṣvantarbhāvādyvāptiḥ /
children.translated_text: Wherever <s>bhāvas</s> (emotional states), as well as semblances of <s>rasa</s> and <s>bhāva</s>, and the quiescence of <s>rasa</s>, <s>bhāva</s>, and their semblances are suggested — there too, the ornaments called <s>preyas</s>, <s>ūrjasvin</s>, <s>samāhita</s>, and others should be applied respectively. Thus, this has been stated with respect to <s>rasas</s> and the like when they are primary. And even when <s>rasas</s> are secondary [to the ornaments], the ornament called <s>udātta</s> (the elevated) has been established by the passage 'and the conduct of great souls' and so forth. Therefore, the suggestive function with respect to <s>rasas</s> and the like is not something separate. Thus, regarding all three kinds of suggested meaning, the sixfold suggestive function demonstrated in the examples just described pertaining to the six kinds — since it is subsumed within the stated ornaments — [there is] proper extension.

children.text:
ṣaṭprakāratā cātra trividhapratīyamānārthaniṣṭhasyāpi vyañjakatvasya vācyasya vivakṣitatvāvivakṣitatvābhyāmukta /
tathā hi---dvividhaṃ vyañjakatvaṃ, vācakaśaktyāśrayaṃ vācyaśaktyāśrayaṃ ca /
tatra vācakaśaktyāśrayamalaṅkārāṇāmeva vyaṅgyatvādekaprakāram /
tatra hyalaṅkārā eva vyajyante, na tu vastumātraṃ nāparasādayaḥ, yaduktam----
children.translated_text: For there, only ornaments are suggested — not mere subject matter (<s>vastu</s>) or <s>rasas</s> and the like. As stated —
"An ornament that is implied is manifested by the power of the word;
since it is not stated by the word, it is born from the power of the word."

And the sixfold nature here is stated with reference to whether the literal meaning (<s>vācya</s>) is intended (<s>vivakṣita</s>) or unintended (<s>avivakṣita</s>), even for the suggestive function pertaining to all three kinds of suggested meaning. For: the suggestive function is twofold — that based on the power of the denoting word (<s>vācakaśakti</s>) and that based on the power of the denoted meaning (<s>vācyaśakti</s>). Therein, that based on the power of the denoting word is of one kind, since only ornaments are suggested.

children.text:
iti /
vācyaśaktyāśrayaṃ tu rasādivastumātrālaṅkārābhivyaktihetutvātrrividham /
tatra yattāvadvācakaśaktyā śrayaṃ vyaṅgyabhūtālaṅkāraikaniyataṃ śabdaśaktimūlānuraṇanarūpavyaṅgayatayā sahṛdayairvyañjakatvāmuktaṃ "sarvaikaśaraṇamakṣayam"ityādau, tatra śabdaśaktyā ye pratīyante virodhādayo 'laṅkārāstatsaṃskṛtasvabhāvaṃ vācyamavagamyete /
ataścatra vācyasya vivakṣaiva /
children.translated_text: Thus. But that based on the power of the denoted meaning is threefold, because it is the cause for the manifestation of <s>rasas</s> and the like, mere subject matter, and ornaments. Now, that which is based on the power of the denoting word, restricted to ornaments alone as the suggested content — which has been said to possess the suggestive function by connoisseurs through its nature as resonance (<s>anuraṇana</s>) rooted in the power of the word — as in '<s>sarvaikaśaraṇam akṣayam</s>' and the like: there, the ornaments like <s>virodha</s> and the like that are understood through the power of the word, and the literal meaning that is understood as having its nature conditioned by those [ornaments] — therefore, there the literal meaning is indeed intended.

children.text:
yattu vācyaśaktyāśrayaṃ "yāte gotraviparyaye śrutipatham"ityādāvasaṃlakṣyakramarasādivyaṅgyaniṣṭhaṃ vyañjakatvamuktaṃ tatrāpi vācyasya vivakṣitatvameva /
vācyabhūtānubhāvādivivakṣayaiva vyaṅgyarasādipratīterutpādāt /
tadevaṃ vācakaśaktyāśrayavyaṅgyabhūtālaṅakāraikaniyate vācyaśaktyāśraye cāsaṃlakṣyakramarasādivyaṅgyaniṣṭhe vyañjakatve vācyasya vivakṣitatvameva /
vastumātrālaṅkāraviṣayasya tu vācyaśaktyāśrayasya vyañjakatvasya pratyekaṃ vācyasya vivakṣitatvāvivakṣitatvābhyāṃ dvaividhyam /
tathāhi 'cakrābhighātaprasabhājñaye'tyādau vastuviṣaye vyañjakatve vācyasya vivakṣitatvaṃ kāryavivakṣāpūrvakatvena kāraṇapratītiprasavāt /
'snigdhaśyāmalakāntī'tyādau tu rāmādiśabdānāmarthāntarasaṃkramitavācyānāṃ vācyamavivakṣitam /
vyaṅgyadharmāntarapariṇatatvāt /
eva vastumātraviṣaye vyañjakatve vācyasya vivakṣāvivakṣe,'laṅkāraviṣaye 'pi vācyaśaktyāśraye vyañjakatve /
children.translated_text: But where the suggestive function based on the power of the denoted meaning, as in 'when the lapse in the family name entered the path of hearing' and the like, pertains to <s>rasa</s> and the like as suggested content in the mode of imperceptible sequence (<s>asaṃlakṣyakrama</s>) — there too, the literal meaning is indeed intended. For the cognition of the suggested <s>rasa</s> and the like arises precisely through the intention of the literal content consisting of <s>anubhāvas</s> and the like. Thus, in the suggestive function restricted to ornaments alone as the suggested content based on the power of the denoting word, and in the suggestive function pertaining to <s>rasa</s> and the like in the mode of imperceptible sequence based on the power of the denoted meaning — the literal meaning is indeed intended. But for the suggestive function based on the power of the denoted meaning that pertains to mere subject matter and ornaments, there is a twofold division through the intention or non-intention of the literal meaning. For: in '<s>cakrābhighātaprasabhā</s>...' and the like, in the suggestive function pertaining to subject matter, the literal meaning is intended, because the cognition of the cause arises preceded by the intention regarding the effect. But in '<s>snigdhaśyāmalakāntī</s>' and the like, the literal meaning of the words <s>Rāma</s> and the like, whose denotation has shifted to another meaning, is unintended — because it has been transformed into another suggested property. Thus, in the suggestive function pertaining to mere subject matter, the intention and non-intention of the literal meaning [obtain]; and similarly in the suggestive function based on the power of the denoted meaning pertaining to ornaments.

children.text:
'lāvaṇyakāntī'tyādau ekasminmanye ityetasminśabde yo viśeṣoktyutprekṣayoranupraveśastadvaśena samāsāditasvabhāvo yo 'sāvekaśabdābhidhānasaṃkarastatpratabhotpattihetuśleṣaprauḍhīkṛtaṃ vācyaṃ vivakṣitam /
tanmūlakatvena rūpakapratīterutpādāt /
children.translated_text: In '<s>lāvaṇyakāntī</s>' and the like, in the single word '<s>manye</s>' (I think), the entry of <s>viśeṣokti</s> (specific expression) and <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) — by virtue of which the nature [of the passage] is conditioned — constitutes a single-word expression-mixture (<s>abhidhānasaṃkara</s>); and the literal meaning, made robust by the <s>śleṣa</s> that is the cause for the arising of that [mixture], is intended — because the cognition of <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) arises on the basis of that [literal meaning].

children.text:
"suvarṇapuṣpāṃ pṛthivī'mityādau tu vācyasyāvivakṣā /
upameyasya bahulābhatvasya tatsadṛśasya yā lakṣaṇā tasyā atyantatiraskṛtavācyamūlatvāt /
yadi tvatra na tiḍantenopamānamastīti dṛṣṭyāta tadbhāvādhyavasānātsuvarṇapuṣpapṛthivīcayanalakṣaṇopamānāvacchāditarūpatvena śūrādiviṣayasya bahūlābhatvasyopameyasya prauḍhoktyā pratipattiḥ, tato 'tra prauḍhoktimātraniṣpannaśarīrasya vācyasyārthasya prādhānyā "dbhede 'nanyatvami"tyevamātmakatayopavarṇitamatiśayoktibhedatvaṃ vācyam /
vyaṅgyā hyupamā tadānīmatra guṇībhavati /
children.translated_text: But in '<s>suvarṇapuṣpāṃ pṛthivīm</s>' (the earth with golden flowers) and the like, the literal meaning is unintended.
