Because the <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (figurative denotation) of the <s>upameya</s>'s abundant availability and of what resembles it has a basis that is an utterly concealed literal meaning. If, however, one takes the view that 'here there is no <s>upamāna</s> through a finite verb form,' then through the determination of identity with that — since the nature of the <s>upameya</s>, namely the abundant availability of heroes and the like, is presented through bold expression (<s>prauḍhokti</s>) as having its form overlaid by the <s>upamāna</s> characterized by the earth with golden flowers, necklaces, and the like — then here the <s>atiśayokti</s> variety described as 'non-difference despite difference' should be stated, since the body of the literal meaning is constituted solely by bold expression and has primacy. For the suggested <s>upamā</s> (simile) then becomes subordinate.

children.text:
evamalaṅkāraniṣṭhasyāpi vyañjakatvasya vācyavivakṣitatvāvivakṣitatvābhyāṃ dvaividhyam /
yatra cāvivakṣā vācyasya vastuniṣṭhe 'laṅkāraniṣṭhe vā vyañjakatve tatra vyaṅgyarasāderjhagityavagamyamānatvādasaṃlakṣyakramatā draṣṭavyā /
yaduktaṃ bhaṭṭavāmanena---"lakṣaṇāyāṃ hi jhagityarthapratipattakṣamatvaṃ rahasyamācakṣate"iti /
ata eva ca sahṛdayairyatra vācyasya vivakṣitatvaṃ tatraiva vastvalaṅkārayoḥ pratīyamānayorvācyena saha kramavyavahāraḥ pravartitor'thaśaktimūlānuraṇanarūpavyaṅgyo dhvanirityuktaṃ, na tu vācyavivakṣāyāmapi /
yatra ca vācyasyāvavakṣā pūrvamuktā "rāmo 'smī'ti 'suvarṇapuṣpā'miti ca tatra vayamadhikāropetaprastutārthānubandhivastūpanibandhādaprastutapraśaṃsābhedatvameva nyāyyaṃ manyāmahe /
yaduktaṃ 'adhikārādapetasye'tyādi /
children.translated_text: Thus, the suggestive function pertaining to ornaments too has a twofold division through the intention and non-intention of the literal meaning. And where the literal meaning is unintended — whether in the suggestive function pertaining to subject matter or to ornaments — there the suggested <s>rasa</s> and the like should be understood as being of imperceptible sequence (<s>asaṃlakṣyakrama</s>), since they are apprehended instantaneously. As <s>Bhaṭṭa Vāmana</s> has stated: 'In <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (figurative usage), the secret is the capacity for instantaneous apprehension of meaning.' For this very reason, the connoisseurs have said that only where the literal meaning is intended does the sequential relation (<s>kramavyavahāra</s>) between the suggested subject matter and ornament together with the literal meaning operate — [and this is called] <s>dhvani</s> (suggestion) whose suggested content is of the nature of resonance (<s>anuraṇana</s>) rooted in the power of meaning — but not where the literal meaning is also intended [in a different way]. And where the non-intention of the literal meaning was stated previously — as in '<s>Rāmo 'smi</s>' (I am <s>Rāma</s>) and '<s>suvarṇapuṣpām</s>' — there, we consider it proper to classify it as a variety of <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant), because of the connection of subject matter accompanied by superimposition with the relevant primary meaning. As stated: 'of what is removed from the topic' and so forth.

children.text:
yattu pūrvaparyāyoktabhedatvaṃ 'snigdhaśyāmalakāntī'tyādau rāmādīnāṃ śabdānāmabhihitaṃ tadupakramamātrarūpatayā draṣṭavyam /
vivakṣitavācyasya paryāyoktabhedatvāt /
yatra khalu vācyavivakṣāpūrvakatvena arthāntaraṃ pratīyate 'cakrābhighāte'tyādāvudāharaṇacatuṣṭaye tatra paryāyoktabhedatā /
paryāyoktalakṣaṇasyāprastutapraśaṃsālakṣaṇavicāravaśena tadyvatiriktaviṣayāvagāhitvāt /
yatra tvavivakṣite vācyer'thāntarasaya pratītistatrāprastutapraśaṃsā /
ataśca paryāyoktāprastutapraśaṃsayoreva yathākramaṃ vivakṣitāvivakṣitavācyayoḥ sarvadhvanibhedasāmānyabhūtayordhvanibhedayorantargatirvācyā /
'suvarṇapuṣpāṃ pṛthivīm'ityādau tu vidarśanābhedatvaṃ yatpūrvamuktaṃ tadadhikāropetaprastutārthānubandhivastūpanibandhātmatvenāsaṃbhavadvācyāyā vidarśanāyā aprastutapraśaṃsābhedatvādupapadyata eva /
etacca vidvadbhirvicārya gṛhītavyaṃ na tvavamṛśyaivāsūyitavyamityalamativacālatayā /
children.translated_text: The classification previously stated in another context as a variety of <s>paryāyokta</s> — as in '<s>snigdhaśyāmalakāntī</s>' and the like regarding the words <s>Rāma</s> etc. — should be regarded as merely preliminary. Because what has intended literal meaning has the nature of the <s>paryāyokta</s> variety. Indeed, where the cognition of another meaning arises preceded by the intention of the literal meaning — as in the four examples in '<s>cakrābhighāta</s>' and the like — there the classification as <s>paryāyokta</s> [obtains]. Because the definition of <s>paryāyokta</s>, through the examination of the definition of <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s>, extends to a domain distinct from that [of <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s>]. But where the cognition of another meaning arises while the literal meaning is unintended — there [the classification is] <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s>. Therefore, the subsumption of all <s>dhvani</s> varieties under <s>paryāyokta</s> and <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> respectively — the two generic <s>dhvani</s> varieties corresponding to intended and unintended literal meaning — should be stated. The classification as a variety of <s>vidarśanā</s> (illustration) previously stated for '<s>suvarṇapuṣpāṃ pṛthivīm</s>' and the like is entirely compatible — because the <s>vidarśanā</s> whose literal meaning is impossible becomes a variety of <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s>, given that the subject matter accompanied by superimposition is connected with the relevant primary meaning. This should be examined and accepted by the learned, and not rejected without reflection — enough with excessive verbosity.

children.text:
tadevaṃ vācakaśaktamūle 'laṅkāraikaniyate vācyaśaktimūle ca rasādiviṣaye vyañjakatve vācyasya vivakṣitatvaikarūpatvam /
vastvalaṅkāraviṣaye tu vācyaśaktimūle vyañjakatve pratyekaṃ vācyasya vivakṣitatvāvivakṣitatvābhyāṃ dvibhedatā /
atastatsamāśrayaṇena trividhapratīyamānārthaniṣṭhasyāpi vyañjakatvasya ṣaṭprakāratā bhavati /
eteṣāṃ ca ṣaṇṇāṃ bhedānāṃ madhyāddvayorbhedayorvācyasyāvivakṣoktā /
caturṣu vivakṣitatvam /
yatra ca vivakṣitatvaṃ tatra vācyasya svataḥsaṃbhavitvātprauḍhoktimātraniṣpāditaśarīratvācca dvaividhyam /
atastatra tasyāṣṭau bhedā bhavanti /
ete cāṣṭau bhedā vācyasya yatrāvivakṣā tadviṣayābhyāṃ pūrvoditābhyāṃ dvābhyāṃ bhe dābhyāṃ saṃkalitāḥ santo daśa saṃpadyante /
eta eva tu padavākyaprakāśyatayā dvaiguṇyaṃ bhajamānā viṃśatirbhavti /
varṇasaṃghaṭanāprabandhādhārasya vyañjakatvasya kṛttaddhitādigatasaya ca padavākyānupraveśenaivāvirbhāvāt /
padaprakāśyatve yathā 'rāmo 'smīti'; /
'cakrābhidhāte'tyādau tu vākyaprakāśyatā /
yathā ca pradhānabhūte vyaṅgye eṣā vyañjakatā rviśatividhā bhavati, tathā guṇībhūte 'pi yathāsaṃbhavaṃ yojyeti /
tadāhuḥ-----
children.translated_text: Thus, in the suggestive function rooted in the power of the denoting word and restricted to ornaments alone, and in the suggestive function rooted in the power of the denoted meaning and pertaining to <s>rasa</s> and the like — the literal meaning has a single form: that of being intended. But in the suggestive function rooted in the power of the denoted meaning and pertaining to subject matter and ornaments, there is a twofold division for each through the intention and non-intention of the literal meaning. Therefore, depending on those [distinctions], the suggestive function pertaining to all three kinds of suggested meaning becomes sixfold. And among these six varieties, in two the literal meaning is unintended. In four it is intended. Where it is intended, there is a twofold division based on whether the literal meaning arises naturally or is constituted solely by bold expression (<s>prauḍhokti</s>). Therefore, there the [varieties] become eight. And these eight, combined with the two previously stated varieties in which the literal meaning is unintended, amount to ten. These very ten, becoming doubled through being manifested by a word or a sentence, become twenty. Because the suggestive function based on the arrangement of phonemes [and] on composition enters [the system] only through words and sentences. As manifested by a word, for example: '<s>Rāmo 'smi</s>.' In '<s>cakrābhighāta</s>' and the like, however, the manifestation is through a sentence. And just as this suggestive function is twenty-fold when the suggested content is primary, so too when it is secondary, it should be applied as appropriate. As they state —
The literal meaning, intended and unintended, in the domain of subject matter and ornament,
in <s>dhvani</s> is intended, [and also] in the domain of word-power and <s>rasa</s>.
In the sixfold division, the literal meaning stated as fourfold intended —
that may be either naturally occurring or fashioned by bold expression.
These are the ten varieties of <s>dhvani</s>; twenty through word and sentence.
In the primary and secondary suggested content, they are generally the same.
Thus.

children.text:
vastvalaṅkāravācye dhvanau pratyekaṃ vācyaṃ vivakṣyamavivakṣyaṃ ceti saṃbandhaḥ /
vivakṣyamiti vivakṣārhamityarthaḥ /
śabdaśaktirasāspada iti vācyakaśaktasamāśrayaṃ rasādivyaṅgyaniṣṭhaṃ ca vyañjakatvamuktam /
tadviśiṣṭaśaktiṃ vyañjakabhūtāṃ rasādīṃśca vyaṅgyabhūtānāspadīkaroti /
evametadyvañjakatvaṃ
children.translated_text: The connection is: in <s>dhvani</s> pertaining to subject matter, ornament, and literal meaning respectively, the literal meaning is intended and unintended. 'Intended' means 'worthy of being intended.' 'In the domain of word-power and <s>rasa</s>' — this refers to the suggestive function that is based on the power of the denoting word and that pertains to <s>rasa</s> and the like as the suggested content. [This suggestive function] makes [both] the suggestive power, which is a special capacity belonging to the suggestive element, and the <s>rasas</s> and the like, which are the suggested content, its abode. Thus this suggestive function
is subsumed within <s>paryāyokta</s> and the like.
This has not been elaborated here at greater length because of the many things that would need to be said.

children.text: kuśāgrīyabuddhīnāṃ hi diṅbhātra evopadarśite sati buddhivallī pratānaśatairnānādigvayāpitvena vistāramāsādayatīti //
children.translated_text: For those of razor-sharp intellect, when merely a hint is shown here, the creeper of understanding extends its spread over a hundred branches reaching in all directions.
From the cloud of the essence of <s>Mīmāṃsā</s>; from the ocean of <s>Pada</s> [grammar]; from the jewel-casket of logic (<s>tarka</s>);
from <s>Murāri</s>, the glory of literary science; from the bee at the lotus-feet of <s>Śauri</s>, the intoxicating flower of the learned;
having heard from the best among the twice-born, <s>Mukula</s>, the ocean of generosity, the irrigating channel of the creeper of fame,
the <s>Koṅkaṇa</s> native <s>Śrī Indurāja</s> composed this short commentary on the <s>Kāvyālaṅkārasāra</s>.
Thus ends the sixth section of the Short Commentary on <s>Udbhaṭa's</s> <s>Alaṅkārasārasaṃgraha</s>, composed by the illustrious <s>Pratīhārendurāja</s>.
